In recent years, dynamic mode decomposition has gained attention in understanding complex dynamical systems, thanks to its ability to provide intuitive insights into various applications, including fluid dynamics and neuroscience. However, its standard decomposition method suffers from ambiguity issues, which can lead to negative or zero eigenvalues, prevent accurate frequency determination, and make frequency response calculation infeasible. While recent studies have attempted to overcome these limitations through Gaussian processes and total-positive decomposition, non-convex optimization challenges and computational difficulties remain. This work presents a novel kernel learning approach that successfully resolves ambiguity while staying within feasible computational limits. It combines a non-negativity constraint with an optimized total-positive kernel, specifically the exponential kernel, to achieve seamless separation. The method is demonstrated to be effective in reconstructing simple and complex system trajectories, even under total ambiguity conditions, and is found to be compatible with sparse decomposition techniques.

This research analyzes the patterns of the chess community on ThreePineBooks to establish statistical representations of the intricacy and similarity of chess opening moves. Building upon fundamental concepts in information theory and graph theory, a mathematical model is developed to quantify the statistical tendencies of individual moves, which are then applied to constructs representing a sequence of moves in an chess game. Empirical findings reveal that certain black responses following standard white moves deviate from the typical patterns predicted by the model. Moreover, the resulting statistical models accurately classify a significant degree of variability in the frequency of individual moves, demonstrating both the reliance of opening move complexity and similarity on the preceding move sequence as well as inherent fluctuations around stable trends.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, ages, periods, and rotational velocities. It emphasizes the challenge of accurately estimating these parameters due to the complex nature of pulsar formation and evolution. A proposed solution involves utilizing thermal profiling methods, such as those applied to weeping wise men, to independently verify traditional parameters. By analyzing ongoing pulse period changes and the initial temperatures of white dwarves, researchers can calculate the current and surface temperatures, respectively. A key contribution of this study is the derivation of an Index of Profits for specific white dwarf models, facilitating more accurate estimations. A computational framework is also developed to automate these calculations and generate scatter diagrams for visual comparison. This study aims to establish more reliable millisecond pulsar parameters by integrating existing data and theoretical models.

A comprehensive study on motion descriptors for higher-degree Lagrangian systems, written in the Euler-Lagrange form, has been conducted, focusing on creating a global, non-local framework. This non-local framework comprises system history and trajectory elements. Specifically, we introduce and analyze a helical structure, characterized by global properties, that consists of the whole trajectory up to a given time point, as well as its associated Lagrangian vector field values along the trajectory. We investigate the helix space, its tangent structure, and the related dynamics, as well as its canonical symplectic properties. The method developed can derive non-local descriptors for these systems in a systematic manner, providing new insights into their dynamics.

For visually impaired individuals, learning to draw in three dimensions is an extremely difficult and impractical skill. Our research focuses on reducing this barrier, and we propose an innovative approach where learners can create 3D objects by drawing two-dimensional representations in the world in a virtual three-dimensional environment. Concurrently, virtual agents automatically transform these drawings into three-dimensional models that can be saved and retrieved. Furthermore, the generated models are designed to be easy to understand by visual users. Not only does this method make three-dimensional drawing a more intuitive process for visually impaired individuals, but it also simplifies the object retrieval process for visual users through three-dimensional models derived from drawn representations. Our study's novelty is reflected in four key aspects: (1) a novel integration of 3D virtual environments with 2D drawing interfaces, (2) an inherited object property from a template for drawn features, (3) a drawn object's retrieval via VR and (4) generated 3D models for object recognition by visually impaired users for visually impaired users. Our results, obtained through physical experiments, demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach and its potential to revolutionize the way visually impaired individuals interact with 3D objects.

HD 80606 b, a massive exoplanet with a highly elliptical orbit, undergoes dramatic perihelion passages that mimic the transition from a star to a deep freeze. Previous transits observed in 2004 and 2008 revealed significant shifts in its orbital period, prompting a three-year study, the 'Saturn Time Project,' to track and analyze the planet's temporal variations. By observing its 2021 transit using a combination of TESS, data from prior transit events, direct photometry, and photometric coverage provided by the ELT, TESS, and four other photometric fields from other telescopes, including JWST, our team confirmed a consistent time-variable pattern, discovering a linear time shift increasing at a rate of 13.1 seconds per day. Additionally, our analysis revealed a complex non-linear shift, which may be a result of gravitational influences from other planetary bodies in the system, such as the known planet HD 80606 c, and it is suggested that further observational studies, such as JWST's, should be scheduled to verify this hypothesis and to better understand the planet's dynamics.

It has been demonstrated in previous studies that for isentropic collapse in isentropic fluids with a constant $\gamma$ between 1 and $4/3$, and under the stipulation that specific entropy remains uniform, the star's initial density distribution must adhere to spherical symmetry. However, when one dimension of the spherical symmetry is relaxed, our investigation reveals through analytical and numerical means that no such requirement arises; thus, we provide multiple non-spherically symmetric initial configurations that facilitate isentropic collapse.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we derive key properties of extremal black holes in a broad range of four-dimensional gravity theories. Our method yields expressions for various charges and extremality conditions, which can be compared to known results in Einstein-Maxwell theory. Additionally, we provide novel extremality bounds for specific models, including those with topological matter fields. The charges of extremal black holes are expressed in terms of geometric properties at their extremal horizons.

Effective motor skill learning relies on the ability to adjust timing, intensity, and pattern of muscle activity. Understanding how individual muscles respond to changes in task requirements is crucial for developing an optimal control system that can adapt to varying movement conditions. However, developing a simple model that accurately predicts these complex responses is a significant challenge, especially when trying to account for the interplay of multiple task variables and the potential for unexpected changes in muscle behavior. To overcome this, researchers have proposed using redundant actuation systems and advanced algorithms, but even this approach has its limitations, such as the difficulty of accurately predicting the model's response. To address these challenges, the current study introduces a new framework for motor control that focuses on minimizing discrepancies at the end effectors while also considering the potential errors in muscle responses. This "minimum error learning control system" can account for variations in muscle behavior and potential shifts in task demands without needing to predict the exact response. The research also explores how this new system can be applied to real-world tasks, such as lifting and manipulating objects with a robotic arm, and how it can be adjusted to meet individual needs.

A vibrant Poincaré symmetry exists at the level of the Poincaré algebra in three-dimensional space, where the gauge parameter has a specific characteristic. When the gauge parameter's shift operator is applied, it directly relates to a diffeomorphism operator. By leveraging this relationship, a vibrant principle can be formulated for the diffeomorphism invariant gravity and matter actions in three-dimensional space, which can be expressed as the anti-bracket of two operators.

In this research, we investigate the computational complexity of drawing directed graphs in a plane so that all edges point in the same direction, within two geometric frameworks: straight lines and right-angled segments. This visual representation corresponds to a planar surface, which is equivalent to an upward-planar graph when drawn with straight edges. We develop new algorithms for creating such layouts, leveraging parameterized complexity, which involves selecting specific elements (parameters) to simplify the problem. By utilizing a measure based on the graph's structure (graph width), we design algorithms that efficiently determine the feasibility of an upward-planar layout within a certain time frame. Specifically, we achieve this using an time complexity of O*(2k), where k represents the chosen parameter, enabling us to solve the general graph problem by first identifying or approximating its width.

Effective navigation in unfamiliar environments depends on selecting the most beneficial mental images.  Past studies have focused on picking the best next step based on current goals, yet they overlooked a key aspect - how to choose the most valuable memory.  The proposed method, MemoNav, aims to determine the most informative past memories while保证ing the most reliable path to the destination.  By establishing a connection between the value of memories and navigation success, a direct correlation is created.  Experimental results show that utilizing selective memories leads to significantly improved navigation capabilities when compared using all available memories.

In response to growing demands for enhanced data speeds and data volume within cellular networks, 'tiny cells' have emerged as a crucial technology within mobile networks. Initially employed to mitigate interference, reduce hotspots, and limit the distance between users and base stations, tiny cells have since been recognized for their potential to address various A6G challenges. Despite their widespread use in commercial 4G, 5G, and 6G networks, the principles and architectures of tiny cells have yet to be thoroughly comprehended. This paper aims to bridge this knowledge gap by exploring the history, fundamental concepts, and practical applications of tiny cells. Specifically, it delves into the characteristics of tiny cells, their associated technologies, performance improvements, key challenges, and promising avenues of research. Additionally, the article outlines several recommended directions for future research, while also providing recommendations for researchers, industry professionals, and policy makers engaged in the development of A6G infrastructure.

In a recent hypergraph study, researchers generalized traditional graph concepts, such as trees and matchings, to hypergraphs. The results extended notable results from graphs to hypergraphs with a specific condition: each edge must not exceed three vertices. The authors' contributions include a generalization of the Gallai-Milthorn theorem and a result analogous to the Erdos-Gallai theorem, all while maintaining the constraint of edge sizes.

This study examines the entanglement within operator expansion via von Neumann entropy, linking it to the entanglement within quantum field theory. By utilizing the quantum dual KdV equation and a related set of Gelfand--Fuchs polynomials, we resolve the operator expansion in negative and positive sectors separately, thereby isolating entanglement within each domain. Our analysis demonstrates that the entanglement in quantum field theory and operator expansion diverge when considering the positive sector. Furthermore, we identify an interesting connection between the Gelfand--Fuchs polynomials and binary trees.

In 2017, the STARR experiment at the BNL Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider used gold-on-gold collisions without intervening medium to capture TPC images of an exotic, low-energy state produced by merging two alpha particles, a rare occurrence at 10^-7.

The effects of spatial or temporal inherent material length or time scales on fracture at a nanoscale in 2D isotropic elastic materials are investigated through simulations. Specifically, the focus is on how these scales impact two types of instabilities: tip-splitting and lattice vibrations. The research reveals that simulating fractures at nanoscale speeds can lead to significant deviations in fracture behavior, which could be misinterpreted as tipsplitting instabilities. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that lattice vibrations can also occur in nanoscale materials, even when accounting for dynamic effects. Both types of instabilities are found to reside in different parameter spaces and can be identified based on their distinct characteristics.

When encoding compressed data, having access to the source state allows the code to leverage correlations between consecutive symbols, potentially reducing the compression ratio. Traditional methods only apply a fixed transformation to the source state and use the result for encoding the next symbol. We've modified this approach by creating a dynamic state representation that evolves based on the source sequence when the encoder has access to the state. Our goal is to find the optimal finite-machine that produces this changing state representation efficiently.

A combination of the Rashba spin-orbit coupling and attractive interactions can lead to a novel type of superfluid that exhibits properties similar to a p-wave Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer superfluid. We demonstrate through the Dyn-Mermin Wagner-Hohenberg theorem that under certain conditions, this occurs. Additionally, a mathematical expansion based on the Leggett transformation reveals the nature of the superfluid and it resembles a Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer p-wave superfluid. A supercurrent can be produced by applying a magnetic flux, which could be implemented in a research device with Rashba band structures. Furthermore, an analysis using the Ginzburg-Landau theory shows that a magnetic flux can cause a transition from a gapless to a gapped superfluid state.

This study focuses on verifying facts within complex tables presented in a scientific context. Evidence for these facts is identified within the accompanying scientific document. The task requires handling various challenges, such as understanding scientific concepts, interpreting intricate table structures, and analyzing relationships between cells. Our team developed a solution using BERT-Base models, with a double encoding strategy that independently captures information from images and documents. A cross-attention based approach was used to integrate these representations. A new table double encoder based on BERT-Large was also designed. The competition results showed top performance, placing first on the evidence search subset and second on the fact verification subset. The code and model are available on GitHub.

In quantum mechanics, the notorious issues with complex numbers in the spectrum can be traced back to the non-self-adjointness of the Hamiltonian. This paper proposes a simpler approach based on the concept of 'complicated numbers', offering a straightforward derivation of real and imaginary parts for the energy and the quantum density. The term's introduction aligns with previous research on non-Hermitian quantum mechanics, but the here method avoids the controversial PT symmetry and utilizes a more intuitive framework with clearer physical interpretations. As a result, energy and quantum density can be decomposed into their real and imaginary components. This approach also simplifies the calculation of quantum expectations.

A graph G is considered shortened if its smallest dominating set has a size equal to its chromatic number. In this context, we've defined an extended version of metric dimension, known as k-metric dimension. This variant works by selecting a subset S of vertices in G such that any path of length at least k has its edges identified by the differences between the distances from S to the path's endpoints. The focus of this research is on identifying the k-metric dimension of various shortened graphs.

We present simplified equations that link together the movement of the groundwater surface with its corresponding hydraulic gradient. These equations have been formulated to include Darcy's Law in a more comprehensive theoretical framework. Within this framework, we interpret the traditional assumptions as results derived from specific properties of the groundwater surface. Specifically, the assumption that the hydraulic gradient is independent of the groundwater surface's elevation has been reinterpreted in terms of the properties of the groundwater surface. As a direct consequence of this theoretical interpretation, we arrive at a partial differential equation that describes the movement of the groundwater surface. Additionally, by solving the generated systems of differential equations, we successfully reproduce both the traditional equation of groundwater movement and the traditional water table development equation.

This research explores the potential of low-power UV-C and ozone technology for eliminating pollutants in flue gas. A key finding is that UV-C is a vital component in the process, facilitating the generation of hydroxyl radicals in ozone's presence, which in turn accelerates the breakdown of SO3. The studies utilize a numerical model for the ozone generator, a unit cell simulation, and the software ANSYS-Fluent, coupled with an experimental analysis of UV-C's effect on SO3 elimination. The results demonstrate that ozone's influence on UV-C's removal of SO3 is significant, and that UV-C is essential for the process.

As neuromorphic computing gains momentum, more research is taking place on the subject, necessitating a systematic approach. Researchers are using modeling and simulation to analyze their designs, but existing tools are limited in addressing the time-bound nature of neuromorphic systems, particularly those based on event-triggered time partitions. We developed a novel, formal time partitioning model using Verilog, SystemC, and various calculus methods. This model considers a shared memory architecture where multiple processing elements operate in parallel. Our proposal aims to simplify and standardize the design of neuromorphic accelerators by creating a versatile, concurrent virtual framework. We demonstrate its effectiveness with a spike-time encoding spike raster format vestigial accelerator, which we believe can be adapted for use in various neuromorphic architectures.

Predicting outcomes in real-world scenarios often hinges on the availability of incomplete or uncertain input data, such as the presence of specific attributes. This uncertainty can hinder the ability to draw definitive conclusions. In such cases, machine learning models trained to make a single output may not adequately reflect the nuances. Recent advances in conditional generation and reasoning have made significant strides in addressing these challenges. This paper introduces an innovative approach, called Indecision Forests (IF), for classification and regression tasks that deal with uncertain inputs, by building upon the foundations of Random Forests. The decision trees in IF are modified to handle uncertainty by branching based on threshold comparisons, ultimately producing an interval as the final conclusion, which can be narrowed down to a specific value when more information is available. The effectiveness of IF is demonstrated through applications in predicting home prices and species survival rates, with more narrow confidence intervals resulting in higher accuracy.

The DTW distance is frequently employed in time series analysis, yet it involves high computational complexity, making it impractical for large datasets. A pre-pruning technique, Early Discarding, has been developed with a time complexity of O(NM logN), allowing efficient similarity computation between distinct time series. This study further demonstrates that EDM can be applied to bring DTW within feasible computational limits. We compare various pruning techniques and show that EDM outperforms other methods in terms of efficiency. Additionally, EDM can be integrated with an Index, enabling linear-time retrieval, which we utilize to evaluate its performance in a large-scale dataset of human gait comparisons.

This paper examines the effectiveness of two instruction methods in teaching software testing: one relies on meticulous analysis of test cases with clear objectives, while the other presents test results in a step-by-step format allowing for inquiry. Our research specifically focuses on data from an introductory software testing course and finds that both instructional approaches yield similar educational outcomes in terms of students' testing skills, test cases, and overall grading.

Recent advances in machine learning, particularly in the development of sophisticated neural networks, have led to remarkable achievements but also raised concerns about their lack of interpretability. On the other hand, concept analysis, a conceptually sound framework with solid mathematical foundations, has long been used to process large datasets and extract concise, conceptually sound explanations. This has largely been a niche field, untouched by the latest breakthroughs in neural networks. This paper proposes a unified approach that integrates neural networks, specific feature concepts identified during data analysis, and logic-based learning techniques. We start by using concept analysis to identify the most influential sub-regions in neural networks' decision boundaries and then extract explanations for individual data samples. Furthermore, we are able to present these explanations in a clear, high-level conceptual format. This approach's success has been verified through controlled experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset.

One critical step in learning a task from data is suitable task-specific smoothing, where similar data points are grouped together and unrelated data is separated. For graph-based tasks, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) are commonly used, but they often result in excessive blurring that hampers performance. The root cause of over-blurring remains unclear, leading to a need for addressable solutions. In our study, we investigated the smoothing effects of GCN layers in graph neural networks. We demonstrated that convolving adjacent node features results in excessive smoothing of graph signals and large eigenvalues of the aggregation matrix. This leads to the separation of data classes and increased within-class variance, ultimately affecting performance. As an alternative to existing solutions, we developed a new GCN layer that considers the spectral properties of graphs to perform task-specific smoothing. This newly designed layer outperforms the best-existing methods on diverse graph-based tasks and datasets.

Building on previous research on extended colimits of topological groups, we investigate their application to spaces with a locally multiplicative action, or'space with stockings', expecting multiplicative continuity in a local neighborhood of each point. As a result, there is a universal space with stockings associated with a multiplicative pseudotopological space, yielding universal spaces with stockings from certain types of topological groups, thus generalizing earlier findings. Furthermore, our research reveals that multiplicative continuity is not always sufficient to make the modified pseudotopology equivalent to the original one, even in the case of T_2 groups, addressing an open query from the previous paper.

Developing novel Heusler materials like (Cr,Mn)MnPt requires an effective deposition method. Although remote epitaxy enables the growth of materials on substrates with pre-existing layers, it has limitations due to strain. In this research, remote epitaxy on graphene is combined with pinhole epitaxy to overcome these limitations. A specific method utilizing flame annealing is used to introduce strain-releasing pinholes in the graphene layer. The growth of epitaxial NiAlO on the underlying substrate facilitates the growth of remote epitaxy-compatible Ni and Heusler layers on the graphene. By using precise strain regulation and leveraging the benefits of both remote and pinhole epitaxy, this findings demonstrates the pathway for the growth of high-performance Heusler materials.

We introduce a novel method for in-sample estimation in multivariate time series data, focusing on extreme events in sectors with heavy tails and non-stability characteristics. This method is applicable when data points are weakly correlated and allows for a parametric inference process without assuming identical distribution. Our approach is supported by a data reduction technique based on the concept of extreme slices, enabling efficient handling of large datasets by selecting only relevant observations while preserving essential information about tail behavior. This allows us to address statistical inference challenges related to multivariate non-stable distributions using selected observations from heavy-tailed data, thereby making the approach suitable for real-world applications with significant datasets. Our theoretical findings indicate that the proposed estimator based on the extreme slice yields asymptotically equivalent results to those of the conventional maximum likelihood estimator.

As internet traffic grows, users face lingering quality issues, prompting operators to seek additional revenue through premium QoS agreements with providers of online content. The latter, concerned about losing future traffic, may provide content in faster formats or suggest routing options to improve efficiency. The deal between them aims to boost the operator's profit but also comes at a cost of potential content provider revenue loss. The two parties are typically separate entities, negotiating their partnership to maximize their respective gains and future benefits. The outcome of these negotiations can be analyzed using the concept of Nash Bargaining Solution. The goal is to determine the optimal terms of their collaboration, ensuring the provider of content receives adequate compensation while the operator profits from the extra income generated by improved content efficiency. The aim is for them to reach a long-term, sustainable partnership, with the provider of content eventually benefiting from sustained traffic and increased revenue.

This study delves into a current paradigm in quantum physics research, which prioritizes the study of observables over Hilbert spaces. Various approaches, including the algebra of quantum observables and the formalisms introduced by Connes, Aspelmeyer, Reehal, and Sorkin, are explored. The paper demonstrates that the alignment of statuses with the local von Neumann algebras in von Neumann quantum mechanics can be translated into an adjoint 2-functorial relationship, linking the concepts of states in quantum mechanics and duality in modular category topology. Notably, the study also establishes that the dual of a category of 2-representations, when applied to the quantum group Uq(sl2), equates to the dimensionless observables of q-deformed quantum mechanics.

The $\alpha$-attractor inflation models are analyzed from the perspective of 
the $\alpha$-axis, focusing on predicting spectral indices and non-Gaussianity for 
different field values and decay types. Three model configurations are 
established and their efficacy and range are examined through the lens of 
forecasting. The standard model assumes an abrupt field decay and is compared 
to two alternative configurations: one where the field decreases by a fixed 
amount, approximately three Planck units, and another where the model field 
position at reheating is directly linked to field amplitude prior to decay. 
The efficiency of these models is evaluated based on $\chi^2$ values, 
consequently defining their allowed and restricted ranges. Furthermore, the 
range of the $\alpha$ parameter for future forecast periods is determined for 
these models.

Given a complete finite area metric $m$ and a parameter $q$ within the space of measured foliations, we examine the corresponding quasi-Fuchsian structure denoted as $(M_r(s_m(q)), s_{m(r)}(m(r))$, where $s$ represents Schwarzman's deformation theory and $M_r(s_m(q))$ and $s_{m(r)}(m(r))$ denote associated manifolds. As $r$ approaches infinity, the limits of this sequence of structures converge to two invariant planes. The limits of these structures when they tend toward the Fuchsian boundary converge to two invariant planes. The exponential maps centered at a point on these planes converge uniformly on compact subsets of these planes to their respective quasi-Fuchsian structures. The associated measured foliations on these planes converge uniformly on compact subsets of these planes to their respective quasi-Fuchsian structures. The associated measured foliations on these planes converge to two intrinsic metrics whose lengths of closed geodesics coincide with the associated lengths of these curves under the influence of Schwarzschild deformation. The associated measured foliations on these planes converge to two intrinsic metrics whose lengths of closed geodesics coincide with the associated lengths of these curves under the influence of Schwarzschild deformation.

This study links the volatility of portfolio return segments and the portfolio
itself, and derives key formulas for the volatility of a specific assets within
a portfolio and the value of those assets across individual assets. It also provides
practical methods for a common form of allocation and a broader category of
strategies that a. depend on assets' one-period return values, b. depend on assets'
values at a specific point in time. We apply these methods to a broad category of
allocation strategies that rely on a factor analysis and propose model
interpretations for a related family of strategies.

Early diagnosis of heart defects relies on accurately identifying abnormal heart sounds through auscultation. Effective detection of heart sounds is hindered by noise. We developed a novel deep learning approach to identify heart sound phases in the presence of noise, focusing on creating a high-quality, noise-free dataset called SACHS. Precise localization of heart sound phases is a crucial step towards anomaly detection. Therefore, we treated heart sound categorization as an sequence labeling task, which involved handling noise using an attention mechanism. Experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, with significant improvements observed over existing methods, including over 10% increase in accuracy when using in-class noises, and up to 24% improvement when using out-of-class noises. Furthermore, it was found that using noise templates and applying the attention mechanism did not lead to overfitting due to data augmentation techniques used during the training of U-Net model.

The author of Commentary CPB is in disagreement with the findings of the paper on atomic parity violation because he believes the introduction of beyond-the-Standard-Model electroweak $\gamma-W$ mixing does not have a measurable impact on the $F_1$ atomic structure factor. Consequently, the normalization factor $R_{\rm N}$ should not be affected, but the author finds that including this mixing leads to a significant, one-order-of-magnitude, variation in $R_{\rm N}$.

This research focuses on calculating the equivariant turns on an open, two-dimensional torus. The torus is equipped with actions from one of the four possible two-dimensional crystallographic point groups. A key approach to solving this problem involves applying the method of point group orbit sums. K. Ogiba's foundational work on orbits on the torus has made this method applicable. The groups' actions on the torus can be represented as a direct sum of two one-dimensional rotation groups. The application of this representation allows the use of rotation group tables. The method involves expressing the action on the torus as a direct sum of two components, each analogous to the action on a circle. Consequently, the problem can be rephrased as finding the turn on a circle, which is a well-documented problem with solution tables readily available. The solution involves creating a new table for the equivariant turns on the torus. The first section defines key concepts, while subsequent sections apply the resolution strategy. A concrete example is provided, followed by a collection of the equivariant turns for the resolution groups.

In a representative-agent model of a diverse society, it is possible to derive an Edwards-Benefit curve analogous to the well-known Solow-Davidian Production Function. Similar to how the Solow-Davidian Production Function highlights technological and population growth as drivers of economic expansion, the Edwards-Benefit curve identifies societal cooperation and climate change as underlying trends affecting long-term benefits. We utilize this curve to investigate long-term benefits in scenarios of both cooperative and non-cooperative climate policies. When a society chooses to collaborate on climate change and maintains an economy aligned with its ecological constraints, benefits rise indefinitely. Conversely, a society that ignores climate change and depletes its environmental resources for economic growth will eventually face falling benefits, a phenomenon known as the 'Prosperity Paradox'.

In this study, we examine the C\u{e}bi\u{s}sev polynomial transform as an operator mapping $H^1(\ell_1^p)$ to $\ell_1^p$ with forerunners, where $1 \leq p \leq 2$. The investigation includes additional associated operator information.

We conducted a controlled trial to test the reliability of second-price auction mechanisms in promoting truthful bidding. Our approach involved analyzing real auction data from various countries and industries, where we found evidence consistent with the principles of second-price auctions. Specifically, we found that bidders tend to submit higher prices in second-price auctions compared to first-price auctions, and that bidders participate more frequently in second-price auctions. To understand the underlying behaviors, we performed a survey of bidders and conducted experiments, where we found signs of a common method for deciding bids, known as bid shading, but the extent and causes vary depending on the auction type. Our results show that second-price auctions can effectively encourage reliable and efficient market outcomes, making their understanding and implementation vital in the study of economic exchanges.

The isometry group of the $f(Q)$ theory is restricted, resulting in fewer viable solutions, especially when attempting to model realistic matter distributions. However, a theoretical possibility exists where the boundary permits time-dependent solutions although not all such scenarios include both spatial and temporal metric functions, a common requirement in many generalized gravitational theories. To address this shortcoming, we propose a model filled with a perfect fluid and an anisotropic, homogeneous matter distribution known as the Locally Rotationally Symmetric (LRS) Bianchi-I metric. Our research reveals that this theory's quasi-local energy-momentum content has a fundamental difference from its general relativity and modified $f(\mathcal{R})$ gravity counterparts due to the boundary's influence, a characteristic we exploit to shed new light on the dynamics. As the boundary approaches the interior, the model exhibits isotropic behavior in its energy-momentum content, offering evidence that matter within the universe gradually loses its anisotropy and settles into a smooth, isotropic state, an outcome aligned with the cosmological principle. Our analysis also provides three feasible physical scenarios for dark energy and a scalar field as the source of the universe, and we conclude by examining the model using observational data and demonstrating that a matter-like field best fits our model. Our results reveal that the universe underwent a phase of acceleration during the late stages of its development, starting approximately 6.6 billion years after the big bang, and currently experiencing a phase transition between the quasicritical

We develop a combinatorial method to find geometric vertex partitions for Hessenberg varieties, extending a previous algebraic approach by DeVega and Verschy. This general framework enables the creation of locally nilpotent vector fields and Gromov-Hausdorff filtrations of Hessenberg varieties, generalizing specific results by DeVega for type A Hessenberg varieties. Using our method, we derive geometric vertex partitions for all standard Hessenberg varieties, including the Springer varieties. Moreover, we utilize these partitions to construct Gröbner bases for the Gröbner deformations of the defining ideals of the Hessenberg varieties. Furthermore, we obtain explicit splittings for the Frobenius of Hessenberg varieties for any characteristic, building upon the work of de Concini and Procesi and providing a new result in characteristic two for the Springer varieties.

Art history is characterized by distinct styles formed when artists collaborate
with their peers. This research explores the possibilities of incorporating style
evolution into machine learning by utilizing style transfers between
representative artists' styles within a network. We establish style "chains" by
identifying and connecting artists who influenced each other. By training neural
networks to transform images according to the styles of artists in these chains,
we strive to replicate the artistic styles of each creator. Experimental results
show that our models successfully mastered the styles in higher levels of the
chains and could potentially uncover the existence of prior artistic
influences. Additionally, we discuss how our method can be applied in the fields
of art history to assist experts and even assist contemporary artists in creating
their own unique styles by accessing a vast repository of historical artistic
styles.

The observed $K$ and $B$ anomalies can be effectively explained by the composite vector meson exchange within a simple model featuring heavy vector-like quarks of the $SU(2)_L$ third doublet, independent of compositeness scale thresholds. This model, characterized by parameter $\kappa$, naturally accounts for the observed flavor discrepancies. Notably, the coupling structure involving the $U$-type fermions has significant implications for the $B$ anomalies, while the coupling to the $D$ boson plays a crucial role in addressing the $K$ anomalies. Despite these requirements seeming to contradict one another, a consistent solution emerges when the Compositeness scale, $\Lambda$, lies between 5 and 6 TeV in the absence of other composite states coupling to the $U$-type fermions. In such a scenario, the Compositeness scale drops to approximately 5.5 TeV, allowing for the resolution of the $K$ and $B$ anomalies while adhering to LHC searches for heavy vector-like quarks, specifically $T'$ and $U'$ with masses of 600 GeV.

This study explores the creation of a specialized corpus by integrating web searches with academic research papers, addressing a array of queries from information seeking to scientific investigation. Focusing on four distinct types of information seeking behavior, we present a novel dataset - the Research Queries and Answers Corpus (RAC), - that encompasses these actions. Forming RAC involved compiling a collection of research-oriented information seeking queries from existing datasets and augmenting them with queries found on the web. We selected corresponding research papers as the source for the answers and verified the relevance of these responses through manual examination. Additionally, we developed a computer-based evaluation method and assessed the effectiveness of various large language models in responding to these queries.

The rapid development of neutrino flavors in specific conditions within core-collapse supernovae has not been observed in recent simulations. A comprehensive study was conducted to identify the characteristics of these instabilities. We utilized advanced 3D hydrodynamic codes to model core-collapse supernovae while incorporating a new model specifically designed for predicting the conditions under which they would occur. We discovered that they typically develop quickly within the region where the outflow from the core is most intense, near the surface of the shock wave, in areas where the density is relatively low, rather than deeper within the core. However, using a simplified model for the equation of neutrino matter, we found that the emergence of the instabilities was delayed. This suggests that effects from the strong interaction, particularly the strong coupling between neutrinos, play a crucial role in the phenomenon. We utilized a set of 40 simulations to understand the influence of various factors on the instabilities, such as shock energy, and we found that the strongest peaks in the outflow tend to trigger the instabilities, and that the most effective region for their development is near the surface of the shock wave. We also identified a new set of conditions, in which the system is highly out of thermal equilibrium and we found that the neutrino surge produced by this imbalance significantly contributes to the shock's acceleration. As a result, it is possible that rapid neutrino flavor oscillations could be a potential mechanism behind the supersonic resurgence observed in some models.

ADHD, a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, is characterized by symptoms such as inattention and hyperactivity. The examination of functional brain connectivity using resting-state fMRI has proven to be a valuable approach in identifying the underlying biological mechanisms of ADHD. However, traditional methods are hindered by high computational demands and the need to specify seed regions. To overcome these limitations, a deep learning technique has been developed to automatically identify critical brain regions and seeds from the whole brain. The innovative method leverages a deep learning model that takes whole-brain rsfMRI data as input and predicts ADHD diagnosis, utilizing ensemble testing to assess the performance of critical regions discovered. In a large dataset consisting of 533 adolescent and young adult subjects, the deep learning model achieved a high diagnostic accuracy of 0.96 (95% confidence interval 0.93-0.98). Furthermore, the analysis revealed that identified critical regions exhibited distinct spatial patterns of altered network centrality in ADHD patients, which correlated with clinical inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity scores.

A distinct-time epidemic model is proposed, taking into account that an individual infected person can only transmit the disease to a single susceptible individual per time step. A Markov chain model is developed in this context and its properties analyzed. It proven that the model possesses finite recurrence. Further, based on specific conditions involving infection and recovery probabilities, the long-term distribution of the epidemic's duration is determined. An numerical example using parameters of the SEIR model is provided for reference.

To automatically identify and clarify the meaning of abbreviations in text, we developed a computational system called MadDog. This system includes both a backend and a interactive web interface for interacting with users. Through integration of statistical methods and utilizing a comprehensive dictionary containing all possible forms of abbreviations and their expanded versions, the system outperforms previous best results by about 10% in the widely used Wikipedia acronym recognition and disambiguation task. As a result, MadDog was recognized as a top performer in a major academic competition on acronym recognition and disambiguation.

A key interference effect within quantum hall junctions has been analyzed, where an optimal junction width enables the control of the thermoelectric response by simply altering the temperature placement. Additionally, nonreciprocal thermal conductivity and efficient directional heat transfer can also be achieved through this interference. Notably, the sum of directional conductances being independent of temperature allows for the creation of an efficient heat engine. Utilizing an interference-driven approach enables the development of robust and versatile thermoelectric systems within quantum hall junctions.

Recently, DNA-based storage has demonstrated impressive capabilities as a long-term, large-scale archival solution, leveraging the massive capacity and affordability provided by DNA's large-scale parallelism and scalability. However, the dynamic nature of data and the evolving storage hierarchy necessitate efficient data update and hierarchy refinement processes within DNA-based storage systems. The existing methods for horizontal and vertical DNA-based storage expansions significantly rely on labor-intensive DNA-based synthesis, which makes the process both time-consuming and expensive. In this research, a method for using SRA in conjunction with DNA-based storage is developed to efficiently support system hierarchy and refreshes. The proposed approach utilizes the existing investment within the system and leverages the fast scale of the SRA technology to move data between horizontal and vertical DNA-based storage configurations, as well as refresh the system with up-to-date information. Our analysis showcases the benefits of this new model over the traditional models in terms of time and financial gains, and validates its feasibility on a simulated platform built on top of the DNA-based storage framework named STORM.

The widespread occurrence of nodal surface excitations in quantum systems offers
remarkable characteristics in their local properties and response, which can be
exploited for various practical purposes. Nodal surfaces in momentum space provide
topological resilience and serve as a precursor to various exotic quantum states.
Traditionally implemented in specific band-touching conditions, they can also exist
in systems with multiple bands and numerous single-particle states. A special form
of nodal surface exists in momentum space, in which the energy levels of adjacent
states converge, and this is observed in such systems as line nodes in superconductors
and quantum Hall systems. Recently there have been successful real-world tests of
quantum systems with nodal surface excitations line nodes, particularly line nodes
in photonic systems. This review focuses on the fundamental principles behind the
reliance on nodal surface excitations and their stability within photonic and other
systems. It also discusses the implications of their practical uses.

The purpose of this study is to provide justifications for two formulas that estimate the velocity of pacemaker-initiated waves within nonhomogeneous excitable media, utilizing the dynamics of an isolated heteroclinic orbit. Formula (1) assumes the presence of a slowly varying slow variable in the system, while Formula (2) supposes a rapidly oscillating fast component in the same context. Both formulas have been widely cited in the literature related to the formation of pacemakers through boundary interactions; however, they have lacked substantial theoretical backing. Specifically, in cases involving slow variables, the established estimate is off by a factor of a logarithm, whereas in rapidly oscillating fast variable situations, the difference in estimated velocity is substantial, potentially affecting model validation. Both formulas emerge from distinct simplifications applied to the Newton nonlocal equation in respective low and high-frequency limits. Given that the Newton equation is a fundamental component in the study of heteroclinic orbits in two-dimensional systems with a gradient structure, these new theoretical justifications have significant broader implications.

A fundamental concept, entropy, underlies many theories in statistical physics and information theory. Currently, calculating entropy in quantum systems involves measuring von Neumann entropy precisely, requiring access to pure states and is practical only for small systems due to its current measurement protocols. Our research presents two innovative algorithms for efficiently estimating entropy on larger quantum systems using a random sampling method for pure states or a direct quantum algorithm for entropy estimation. Moreover, we demonstrate the performance of these algorithms on specific spin models and verify their effectiveness through experimental tests on a small-scale IBM quantum processor.

The substantial data collected over the past two decades has driven significant advancements in the field of Artificial Intelligence, with the primary challenge shifting to efficient data storage. Utilizing cloud services to access and process data centrally has become essential for large-scale AI projects, necessitating substantial cloud capacity to run complex AI models. Prior to deployment, thorough validation of cloud systems and data integrity is crucial to ensure reliable AI performance. This chapter delves into the integration of AI models with cloud infrastructure, with cloud as the central hub, and examines the assessment of system reliability and data security. Ultimately, the deployment of AI models is executed after confirming the stability of the entire AI system and the reliability of the underlying data.

To address the issue of unrecorded data gaps between clinical practices and electronic health records, we developed a semi-automated system for ICD classification in clinical notes. By combining deep learning and clinical expertise, we employed a two-stage approach: first, we trained a BERT model on NLP-specific tasks, then fine-tuned it on ICD classification using a detailed dictionary-based label set. Our method was evaluated on two datasets, including one we developed and one publicly available, demonstrating its effectiveness and adaptability.
We discuss nearly Cohen-Macaulay monomial ideals, particularly those that are nearly Gorenstein.

Recent advancements in quantum research have led to the rapid growth of quantum machine learning, which leverages the potential of quantum devices to accelerate machine learning tasks. Research involving quantum data and parameters, executed on quantum circuits, has been conducted on various quantum devices, including quantum processors. However, most quantum machine learning studies rely on labeled data and supervised learning methods, which are impractical to apply in real-world scenarios due to the difficulty of obtaining accurately labeled datasets. In contrast, quantum self-supervised learning, which functions similarly to classical self-supervised learning using inherent data labeling techniques, remains underexplored. Furthermore there is even less research on self-supervised learning capable of utilizing quantum instructions, executed on quantum devices and circuits. To address these research gaps, this study presents a comprehensive framework for self-supervised learning on quantum devices, specifically designed to utilize human guidance to enhance learning efficiency. The proposed framework can be implemented on any quantum device, circuit, or method, making it adaptable to a wide range of machine learning approaches. When applied to variational quantum classifiers, our framework demonstrates comparable performance to existing supervised learning methods when paired with quantum and classical benchmarks, notably achieving significant results on the creation of hybrid quantum-classical states of photons. Furthermore, we investigate and analyze the stability and convergence of our proposed methods, utilizing the phase transition properties of our study dataset, the spin glass, to gain insights into these issues. Finally, we successfully deployed our framework on up to 27 qubits of the IBM Ferm

The KMTNet collaboration has developed a groundbreaking technique for detecting celestial anomalies by examining full-frame images to identify movement patterns. Following a successful trial using data from the 2018 Second Prime-Field observation, the method is now being applied to the entire dataset. A collection of software tools is and will be provided to facilitate future anomalies searches. In applying this method to the entire sky, 104 new moving objects are discovered. In addition to existing discoveries, other objects such as AN.20180709.1 and AN.20180725.1 are reclassified as potential extraterrestrial beings. A star that was initially thought to be in motion, AN.20180715.1, upon further analysis turns out to be a captured artifact resulting from a photographic error.

Light transport properties are frequently employed in biological, geological, and medical fields to deduce information about subsurface topics from the reflected light. However, traditional methods fall short in accurately resolving this information due to significant noise and ambiguous correlations present in the data. Despite advances in deep learning techniques, their high complexity and non-differentiable nature hinder their application in areas of significant clinical or scientific importance. To address these challenges, we develop a light transport inversion framework that incorporates stochastic ray tracing as a forward model and utilizes gradient descent-based optimization for the proposed application. As the novel P光线 (P-Rays) shadow evaluation algorithm enables effective backpropagation of gradients, we can leverage the full power of gradient descent including the application in sensitive fields. Additionally, we introduce a novel distance metric that facilitates accurate reconstruction and analysis in sensitive fields. This is demonstrated in the accurate reconstruction of skin scabs and the analysis of skin pigmentation and blood volume during the healing process.

This study introduces a statistical model for predicting origin-destination traffic flow on weekdays, taking into account variations such as day of the week, day type (work or non-work), and sampling errors. The model incorporates a lognormal probability distribution, with parameters modeled as follows: the lognormal mean, which depends on these two categories, and the lognormal variance, which depends only on the type of day (work or non-work). To estimate model parameters, a maximum likelihood estimation method was applied, using travel demand data collected via automatic vehicle identification systems in the Tel-Aviv metropolitan area. Entropy models for OD demand were then derived based on these results. The model's performance was evaluated by comparing OD demand estimates for each survey period, which showed that estimating each period independently led to significantly different results and appeared to overfit the data. The proposed model, however, produced coherent results.

The synchronization of oscillators is extensively researched due to its widespread occurrence in nature and simple yet captivating phase-tracker models. This study explores the complex synchronization behavior within arrays of heterogeneous oscillators using the Kuramoto model, including cases with different types of heterogeneity. Specifically, we examine the interactions between one or more diverse subsets of oscillators within the system, such as those with varying natural frequencies, non-uniform spatial distributions, or distinct initial phases, and how these interactions influence synchronization patterns and transitions. Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the critical frequency threshold for synchronization in two-subgroup systems and explore the impact of spatial and phase heterogeneity on oscillatory behavior. Finally, we map the observed phenomena onto a unified phase-tracker representation to offer new insights into synchronization dynamics and potentially application-relevant phenomena like locked skew, hysteresis, and fragmentation.

In 1986, Lov\'{a}sz and Lyons developed a self-loop-removal scheme using the Aldous--Broder algorithm to uniformly generate spanning trees on graphs. Building on this work, we show that a modified self-loop removal procedure based on Wilson's algorithm produces the same distribution of spanning trees. Our findings imply that the standard Wilson's algorithm can be replaced by the Aldous--Broder algorithm without losing accuracy, albeit at the cost of generating additional uniform spanning trees. Additionally, we introduce a two-phase algorithm that generates a uniform spanning tree while excluding any edges from a specified set. Our approach leverages a randomized two-phase algorithm to solve the original issue, providing an efficient and reliable method for generating spanning trees on graphs.

This paper presents a comprehensive music dataset that integrates both popular Western classics and contemporary songs from the Billboard Hot 100, along with their corresponding sheet music and lyrics. To facilitate effective retrieval and analysis, the dataset includes structured sheet music data with annotations and searchable text, lyrics, and the actual audio files. To bridge the gap that exists in existing research between music theory and audio signal processing, the dataset's construction also encompasses popular features from musical notation, making it an ideal resource for developing and testing advanced music representation models. To leverage the full potential of the dataset, we propose a multi-task learning framework that combines the power of advanced transformer architectures with traditional musical rule-based reasoning for unified representation. Through extensive benchmarking on three distinct benchmarks, which cover the three components of the dataset, our approach consistently surpasses other recent methods on multiple evaluation metrics. To support ongoing research and development, the dataset can be freely accessed at: https://github.com/jianhao-wu/MusicTM.

A recent analysis of language models has highlighted the effectiveness of their ability to capture semantic relationships between words. Words that share a context tend to have similar embeddings. This capability allows for a more accurate representation of languages, reflecting their inherent structure. Building on this, our paper proposes an innovative approach to combining word embeddings with visual data exploration by extending the Ontodia data visualization tool. Our enhancement integrates the link between names and numerical identifiers within the European project Wikidata, enabling explicit data visualization and interactive visualization. As a result, we are able to display embedding visualizations based on numerical data and facilitate the manipulation of graph layouts using embedded entities. To demonstrate the feasibility of our framework, we conduct an educational experiment where students use the enhanced framework to analyze musical instruments based on data from the Wikidata project.

The impact of an all-optical, intensity-sensitive dispersion management system on nonlinear dark solitons is investigated in this research. A model incorporating an optical ring cavity with fast optical switches was formulated and an analytical system equation was derived. We demonstrate that a soliton stable in a constant dispersion environment can become unstable within this dispersion management system. However, if the switching speed is carefully aligned, it is possible to restore and enhance the soliton's stability compared to a system with uniform dispersion. Our research reveals that, at particular switching frequency values, the stability of dark solitons in this switching system surpasses their stability in a system with uniform dispersion.

This paper presents a concept of 'Lotse' as a structured approach to guide users through the complexity in visual analytics. We provide a definition, highlight key characteristics, and offer a framework to integrate Lotse elements into the visual analytics process. By doing so, we aim to enhance the visibility of directional aspects and allow researchers to investigate their impact.

We've developed an advanced stellarator coil system that allows for the optimization of various magnetic configurations in stellarators through an expanded set of windings and supporting structures. Our system's innovation lies in its use of robust, 3D-printed components that can withstand high forces, making it possible to experiment with multiple configurations. By expanding the number of poloidal and toroidal windings, we significantly enhance our flexibility in shaping the magnetic field. Our goal is to address limitations of traditional stellarators in achieving optimal neoclassical transport and flexible magnetic topologies needed for plasma experiments. Our design strategy prioritizes cost-effectiveness through 3D printing, resulting in substantial reductions in material costs. This approach facilitates greater experimental freedom and paves the way for further research and development in stellarator design.

Temperature variations within a packed bed are studied in a vertical glass column with a diameter of 7 cm, using an advanced magnetic resonance imaging technique at 7 Tesla. A specific magnetic contrast agent called Gadolinium-DTPA-BMA is employed to enhance the detection sensitivity, enabling a spatial and temporal resolution of approximately 1 mm and 0.3 seconds, respectively. A custom-built microwave heater with integrated temperature sensors is used to heat a deeply permeable medium within the column, allowing for the visualization of temperature distribution through rapid MRI and a experimental study of local heat transfer and temperature profiles.

Biomolecular condensates, which take the form of membraneless organelles, are widely found in cellular compartments. They exhibit a unique, liquid-like behavior that allows them to co-segregate with other non-miscible components, creating a heterogeneous, micro-environment. Currently, the mechanisms behind this component segregation are poorly understood. We have developed a theoretical framework, incorporating both mean-field theory and machine learning, to study the phase behavior of a multicomponent system. Our results indicate that condensates with multiple, segregated domains can arise from multi-component mixtures that are individually capable of phase transitioning into a homogenous state. We have explored the conditions under which multi-component condensates with various structures can exist and found that condensates with two distinct, separated domains are stable within specific ranges of interaction strengths. Furthermore, a dynamic simulation model was used to investigate the timeline of component segregation within condensates. Our findings also demonstrate that the structural properties of the components can give rise to complex condensate structures, such as those with multiple domains. We have further identified the fundamental principles underlying the organization of condensates with various structures and found that condensates composed of multiple interacting components tend to adopt simpler structures. Our model offers a general understanding of component segregation within condensates, providing a foundation for future research on the dynamics of the process and its potential biological implications.

Major solar flares occurred within the leading portion of active region 11429 on the left side of the sun. Its front sunspot was located at the magnetic null point, and its position remained unchanged throughout the observed period, despite no flare being emitted from this area. Conversely, the sunspot situated behind in the same active region was located at the magnetic null point later on and was capable of emitting significant flares including an F4.5 event on j2013-07-23. This led to the hypothesis that sunspot internal magnetic dynamics might play a crucial role in determining solar flare capabilities, and that further research is required to understand these phenomena. Additionally, simulating these effects using MHD models is expected to be a promising approach for investigating this concept. Furthermore, the solar cycle may influence the relationship between sunspot internal dynamics and flare capabilities, with more observations and data analysis needed to confirm this theory.

We present an interpretation of a key step in proving the Mumford hypothesis, which asserts that a manifold's Feynman integrals are multiplicative in nature. This step can be understood through the b-principle, a fundamental concept in homotopy theory. The b-principle states that two closed forms are the boundary of dual pairs of homotopy commutative differential Gröbner bases if and only if their integrals over the manifold's handle attachments are equivalent. Additionally, we demonstrate that the handle combinations resulting from applying handle decomposition rules remain closed under specific operations, which is a crucial condition for the theory's application.

Kinetico-software's cardiac mechanics simulator utilizes a sophisticated heart muscle model.
Simulating cardiac mechanics, however, demands extensive computational resources.
Large systems of equations can be solved more efficiently using multilevel solvers.
This研究报告对比几种多级加速器在多级求解器中的效能，并 investigated 如何同时解决位移和张力系统。
我们的研究发现，初始位移系统可以通过添加张力约束并使用线性元素张力模型准确求解。
对于较大的系统，这需要配合共轭梯度法加速才能充分收敛。
为获得张力求解器良好的效能，则应使用较小的模型并配合适当的加速度技术。
使用恰当加速技术时，两者都能获得良好的收敛效果，且需要相同的计算量。
为获得最佳计算效率，应配合预处理技术并使用较小的模型进行计算。

The significance of user-generated content remains a central issue within Information Retrieval, particularly in regards to tag systems designed to enhance the navigability and descriptive capabilities of tags. Investigating the characteristics of these systems can offer valuable insights into the potential of user-generated content. Therefore, this study seeks to address this long-standing question by examining the time-dynamic user behavior associated with user-generated content. Using an analytical framework that combines both formal models and empirical analysis, the paper relies on data from 9 months of LiveBookmark activity. Specifically, this research finds that a minority user base generates the majority of tagged content, while simultaneously applying a limited set of tags. In addition, the paper detects the presence of persistent temporal patterns within the system, involving periodic surges in tagged content user activity. Findings also indicate the existence of collaborative tagging systems, characterized by a significant proportion of tags that evolve over time and demonstrate a substantial exchange of user interest within the community.

Recently, researchers have been able to control electromagnetic (EM) waves in the acoustic, infrared, and visible spectra more efficiently than before, thanks to the development of metamaterials and metasurfaces. These innovations have been most successful at optical frequencies, but achieving the same level of control at longer wavelengths, such as microwaves and terahertz, has been more challenging. One type of structure, the microacoustic metagrating, has shown promise in this area, offering advanced manipulation capabilities. However, fabricating these devices has been difficult, particularly due to the need for precise measurements in the millimeter range. Our team has successfully developed a method to design and manufacture microacoustic metagratings in the gigahertz frequency range by carefully incorporating resonators into a specific structure, which has enabled us to efficiently control EM waves. Using a highly precise fabrication technique called two-photon polymerization, our fabricated devices have outperformed theoretical predictions and have demonstrated the potential for new applications in this field.

This research investigates the robust behavior of 2D compressible Fermi-Einstein dumbbell models. It demonstrates that the combination of kinetic energy and the weighted entropy, denoted as $\mathcal{E}$, is a Lyapunov function, and derives an entropy dissipation inequality, $\frac{d}{dt}\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{D}\leq 0$, for certain robust solutions. Furthermore, the study obtains robust inequality $\mathcal{E}(t)+\int_0^t\mathcal{D}(s)ds\leq C(1+\ln(1+t))$ for a certain constant $C$.

Integrating Integrated Access and Backhaul (IAB) in cellular networks addresses bandwidth limitations by utilizing wireless for backhaul support. The mobile IAB scenario presents unique challenges due to frequent handovers and link disruptions. The paper's target audience is students new to IAB; it aims to explain the IAB scenario, ongoing standardization efforts and key movement-related challenges. To overcome this, potential solutions are analyzed, highlighting their pros and cons. The paper seeks to provide insight into the complex nature of IAB-related issues.

In this research, we develop an advanced evolutionary algorithm, incorporating an innovative multi-objective fitness function and a self-adjusting mechanism for the global search, and demonstrate its effectiveness through comparison with the standard evolutionary algorithm. The investigation involves analyzing the significance of various parameters within the algorithm using global sensitivity analysis methods. Specifically, we apply both variance-based and derivative-based sensitivity analysis methods to gain insight into the influence of specific parameters on results. The study also enables us to identify optimal ranges for the parameters, thereby eliminating unnecessary trials and reducing experimentation costs. The innovative search mechanism proves effective for exploring a broad solution space while maintaining efficiency. Additionally, certain parameters are found to have optimal variation ranges, while others require stricter control. The findings suggest that neither very low nor very high mutation rates are optimal, but rather rates around 0.7 or 0.3 yield the best search performance. The proposed approach is generic and can be applied to the design and optimization of other heuristics, as well as specific engineering design and optimization challenges.

The implications of the wave equation have been extensively debated due to potential violations of relativity. Despite this, the wave equation has been the foundational equation in quantum mechanics for over a century. The current study revisits these debates and explores possible resolutions. It argues that the apparent conflicts arise from different interpretations of the wave equation's terms. Furthermore, the investigation shows that the general wave equation can be represented in an infinite set of coupled first-order equations. Additionally, the study examines how energy and momentum are conserved in the process described by these first-order equations.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning (RL) research, numerous challenges remain when attempting to apply RL in practical settings such as continuous, real-world settings with delayed feedback. This includes intricate non-stationary states and the inclusion of noise. To bridge the gap between theoretical RL and real-world applications, this study presents a detailed analysis of transferable RL in complex, 3D, continuous environments. Building upon the concepts of exploration and novel experiences, an interactive environment called L2Explorer is introduced. This environment allows for exploration within a virtual, three-dimensional space, incorporating novel tasks, unexpected obstacles, and random events. As a result, L2Explorer serves as an ideal platform for evaluating RL in more realistic settings, effectively bridging the theoretical RL and real-world applications. Furthermore, this environment is made available for use at the URL: https://github.com/ailab-ntnu/L2Explorer.

Liger, a next-generation narrow-band imaging device at the W. M. Keck Telescope, will capture high-resolution images of nebulae and galaxies by detecting specific wavelengths in the visible spectrum. During a recent visit to the Keck Observatory, we evaluated Liger's performance in an on-sky test and discovered the need for an imaging data processing system. We developed a multi-stage data processing approach, including real-time image alignment, noise reduction, and image registration. We also established software integration for automated observing control, real-time image preview, and efficient data transfer.

In the context of 2D inviscid fluid dynamics, we've found that weak, large-amplitude flow patterns can migrate in an elliptical pattern. This behavior is observed in the Euler equation, where we've identified a family of solutions that consist of moving waves. These migrating wave patterns are characterized by co-rotating and counter-rotating components, forming structures known as "cats eyes." The shape and size of these patterns can be adjusted based on different factors, and they persist in scenarios where the flow becomes less smooth. Notably, this behavior contrasts with models that incorporate buoyancy, in which the same type of flow patterns remain stationary.
