This study investigates a class of deterministic kinetic growth equations influenced by the maximum principle. We initially prove the existence and uniqueness of weak solutions to these equations in their original nonlocal form. Subsequently, under specific conditions, we demonstrate convergence to a quasi-geostrophic equation in the form of kinetic transport with a drift term.

In times of crisis such as COVID-19, governments and decision-makers require reliable data and insights to make informed decisions. Unfortunately, existing data sources often fail to provide the needed support due to limitations, leading to a reliance on ad-hoc information collected through social media and web searches. These efforts require significant time and expertise, posing a challenge for public sector organizations. 

To address this issue, we introduce a data analysis system tailored for use by these organizations. By leveraging historical data and the knowledge of COVID-19 spread and behavior in the specific region, our system processes real-time information collected from a web search to provide valuable insights. These insights aid the organizations in monitoring the epidemic's progress and identifying changes in people's behavior, thus enabling them to adjust their policies and measures as needed. 

The system was put into practice through a collaboration with the Department of Science and Innovation (DSI) in South Africa, where we combined the information from a specific web search with their internal knowledge and expertise. This resulted in the creation of a dashboard that provides insights and forecasts the COVID-19 cases for a period of two weeks.

A set of integers, denoted by A, has a sumset, A + A, which we aim to characterize. Our objective is to identify sets, particularly those with a small number of elements representing the sumset, that satisfy this condition. We seek to prove an overarching interpretation of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem in this regard. The theorem's proof relies on an overarching strategy, including an overarching lemma applicable to all cases and two critical technical technical technical lemmas technical lemmas.

Diagnosing and monitoring glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy are challenging due
to their shared requirement for regular eye examinations. These professions
are difficult due to their significant impact, necessitating accurate
diagnosis. Detecting glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy in the early stages can
significantly improve patient care. Recent advancements in deep learning
techniques, particularly in their application to retinal image analysis, have
revealed their potential in automating this process. The combination of multiple
input sources, such as clinical measurements and retinal images, has
demonstrated superior diagnostic capabilities. In contrast to existing studies
focusing on individual tasks, we address this issue by developing a dual-task
neural network that simultaneously identifies diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma.
This is achieved through the integration of unmodal data (posterior chamber
intraocular pressure) and a retinal image. Our approach leverages the information
contained in a retinal image to enhance the interpretation of the clinical
measurement and uses a glaucoma detection neural network. This is complemented
by a diabetic retinopathy detection neural network. We experimentally verify the
effectiveness of this model and find that it outperforms current practices.

X-ray analysis of patients by AI could help triage those at high risk of intensive care unit admission, with the current study investigating the link between COVID-19 radiological features and ICU admission severity. Analysis of 5,123 annotated patient chest X-rays, categorized into COVID-19 severity, revealed commonly affected areas and patterns such as opacities, consolidations, and specific lung lobe involvement. Results showed distinct areas of concern for non-ICU and ICU patients, with further subdivision based on disease severity. Tertiary analysis identified 'edge cases' not typical of their assigned category. These findings support the development of AI models to predict ICU admission from chest X-rays, with potential to inform clinical practice and improve patient care.

This research focuses on determining the boundaries of transmission eigenfunctions within a medium of varying density, using numerical methods and an analytical approach. Our goal is to derive a formula that can automatically identify these limits by solving an associated eigenvalue problem. An numerical algorithm has been developed to implement this theory in practice. Experimental data have been generated to validate and illustrate the method's effectiveness. Moreover, an analytical transmission eigenvalue problem has been derived, yielding exact solutions. These solutions have been utilized to evaluate the accuracy of our numerical solutions.

Reinforcement learning from imaginary data is a computationally efficient method for policy learning that simulates actions without the need for real interactions, ideal for scenarios with high interaction costs. The core challenge lies in effectively representing the agent's goals to guide exploration. Existing techniques rely on imaginary data collection, but achieve limited success due to poor goal representations and inadequate filtering of irrelevant data. To address this, we propose a two-fold solution: employing pre-trained models to enhance goal representations and developing a data quality assessment mechanism through contrastive learning. This is accomplished by pre-training models on large, unpaired datasets, incorporating them into the ITLR framework, and designing a contrastive learning approach to identify and discard redundant goal states, ultimately improving policy performance.

The global simplicial abelian group formation, denoted $\coprod$, represents the universal solution to the problem of constructing a simplicial group from any given simplicial abelian set. This construction, $\coprod: \mathsf{sSet} \to \mathsf{sGrSet}$, is also the left adjoint to the forgetful functor, reflecting the universal property. The formula for the group addition in the simplicial set $X$ is $\sigma \mapsto \sigma \oplus \sigma' \mapsto \sigma \odot \sigma'$, where $\odot$ represents the pointwise sum.

For a finite group G, let's consider the maximum number of subgroups it can contain, which we'll call h(G). This maximum is influenced by the minimum order of the elements within G, denoted as k. It has been proven that this maximum is bounded above by the equation: a_0 + a_1 b + a_2 b^2 + ... + a_i b^i, where the a_n coefficients satisfy the condition a_n <= n! (n + 1)^k - 2. The result generalizes an earlier work of G. Higman on determining the maximum number of subgroups in a finite p-group of a given index.

This study reexamines the absorptance formulas proposed by Absormet for the H2 detector, comparing theoretical models with Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis reveals that the existing H2 formula overestimates absorptance by 10-20% for 800 eV photons and 30% for higher-energy photons. We also identify previously unaccounted-for contributions to absorptance in the H2 formula, amounting to 20% for 800 eV photons and increasing with energy. In contrast, the process described as "Compton loss of escape" contributes maximally 5% to absorptance across the 800 eV to 3 keV range. These discrepancies likely explain the excessive noise and excessive absorptance loss observed in H2 data, particularly in domains with high energy deposition rates, where it may be responsible for up to 50% loss. To mitigate the original H2 formula's limitations, a revised approach is proposed, leveraging an updated model accompanied by individual corrections for each component.

The Visual Relationship Detection task in computer vision is all about identifying objects and relationships between them in an image. Current methods using deep neural networks are limited in their performance, with inaccurate findings often limited by the resolution of the image. Our proposal involves a new approach to tackle the challenge of misclassified relationships, with a focus on spatial information and multi-level features. We also use data augmentation methods to manipulate image size, resolving the resolution limitation issue. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on the MS-COCO dataset and provides an effective solution for the problem of misclassified relationships.

The weak measurement in quantum theory has long been linked to the strong measurement through the concept of quantum instruments.  However, the connection cost between these 'weak' and 'strong' measurements has yet to be determined.  In this research, the connection cost is defined for various scenarios, including measurements of states, quantum channels, and even general quantum operations known as superchannels.  The connection cost of feeble measurements is shown to be at least as great as the minimal amount of memory required to apply a quantum operation.  Additionally, the connection cost is calculated for several scenarios, including measurements of pure states, channels with rank-one outputs, and more complex scenarios, yielding connections close to the minimum possible.  Furthermore, the connection cost of applying a channel is proven to be equal to its information dimension, a result with implications for the quantification of quantum correlations.

Social network analysis is the process of applying graph methods to data related to human interactions. Typically, this involves using a small subset of the Delbert Kleinberg's original model, which, however, is insufficient for real-world social data analysis. In this paper, we introduce The Complete Network (TCN), a probabilistic model that captures the full complexity of Delbert Kleinberg's original framework. By using the TCN, we can effectively reconstruct the social network from Delbert Kleinberg's data while also generating a set of attributes that explain the observed relationships. Furthermore, we refine the TCN into a complete social relationship model and prove its uniqueness. In contrast, existing social network models are only approximations of the TCN and can be derived from it. Lastly, we demonstrate the efficacy of TCN in producing graphs that accurately represent real-world social data.

Recent deep learning models have achieved great success in various visual recognition tasks, yet most rely on independent pixel analysis and limited interaction. Some pioneering works have employed deep convolutional neural networks (CNN) and non-local operations to capture long-range dependencies, but their structural designs can be complex and lack explicit connections. Our proposed Active Graph Message Transfer CNN aggregates global image information, initially by arranging pixels into a 2D grid, then constructing a graph with an interactive learning process. We establish long-range dependencies between distant pixels, allowing a more transparent and straightforward structural design. Our model exhibits superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods, and our approach offers a more interpretable understanding of the interplay between spatial location and feature learning. Our results also demonstrate the significant benefits of considering long-range dependencies in these networks.

This paper explores the design of digital constant multiplication units, focusing on multiplying by constants such as 3, 5, or 7, which typically require an extra addition operation in hardware and can be space-intensive on integrated circuits due to area constraints. A new design method is proposed that allows for efficient hardware implementation of these operations by reusing adder components, serving as a building block for more complex constant multiplication circuits. The paper also discusses the design of control logic for enabling or disabling the extra addition operation and uses a systematic approach to determine the optimal number of adder stages. Three types of control logic designs are identified and analyzed, resulting in optimized hardware for the desired functionality. Notably, the paper presents an optimal 30-bit hardware design for a 4-input constant multiplier, achieving a 20.5% area saving compared to industry standard designs.

Quantum machine learning has emerged as a rapidly evolving area within quantum computing research, driven by the potential for significant speedups using theoretical quantum algorithms. Among these, quantum neural networks have been proposed as a way to integrate quantum computing principles into machine learning models. This paper explores the dual perspective of quantum neural networks, examining the advantages they offer in hardware implementation as well as design flexibility. It summarizes current quantum neural network models from multiple viewpoints and discuses key challenges hindering progress in the field.

Research on radio-frequency (RF) RF cavities and structures is instrumental in both classical and modern accelerator technology, spanning classic and advanced applications such as RF power amplifiers, beam-cavity interaction, and high-power test facilities, among others. Low-beta, medium-beta, and high-beta RF cavities are typically investigated in the context of linear accelerators and colliders, whereas Radio Frequency Near Room Temperature (RF CRT) cavities are usually studied in circular accelerators. Additionally, radii research, beam-cavity interaction, beam loading, beam breakup, and beam pipe research are also vital areas of study in beam physics. On the other hand, RF cavities and structures are also central to many applications in industry and technology, including the design of radio frequency near-room temperature cavids and beam physics related topics such as beam loading, beam breakup, and radii research.

The potential for a muon collider to explore high-energy physics has garnered significant interest within the scientific community. However, the transition from a concept to a realistic feasibility study still requires substantial effort. Recently, this goal has been advanced with the establishment of a working group by the muon community. The group has specifically focused on refining production cross sections, developing a detailed cost timeline, and outlining a path toward a comprehensive muon collider feasibility report. This paper serves as an introduction, introducing the fundamental challenges and problem areas associated with muon collider schemes. It also highlights the current status and progress made in each stage of the muon collider process: acceleration, pion/deutons stripping, and low-energy positron collider. The study compares the characteristics of neutrino beams, positron beams, and the corresponding electromagnetic showers as they emerge from the target. The analysis specifically examines the acceleration process from the production threshold all the way up to multi-TeV collider energies, taking into consideration various accelerator technologies, including radio-frequency linacs and superconducting ion sources versus regenerative superconducting radio-frequency cavities and deuton targets, as well as superconducting wire brakes and target options. The study also discusses beam-based and beam-based detectors, as well as beam-induced electromagnetic showers, and how a muon collider could potentially serve as a multi-beam, multi-probe facility for studying several types of new physics beyond the standard model.

We have derived dispersion relations for relativistic fluid dynamics in a relationship with the Knudsen number and viscosity coefficients. These relations serve a similar purpose to the relativistic Navier-Stokes equations but with fewer constraints. The derived dispersion relations allow for a nuanced understanding of viscosity's effect on stability, rendering some previously invalid conclusions due.

The early universe's first seconds may have produced black holes of up to 10^15 grams, known as primary black holes, through unusual fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background. As these black holes collapse, they may generate high-energy particles, including neutrinos and antineutrinos, around them, which would otherwise be indistinguishable from the cosmic neutrino background. To better understand the effects of these black holes, researchers are analyzing the impacts of these high-energy particles on neutrino detectors and the cosmic microwave background, which would provide evidence for these black holes through the distortions they create in the early universe.

We have developed the Virtual Protected Framework (VPF), a novel architecture for processing data using computation frameworks based on Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE).
VPF can execute any program written in C efficiently, even with some minor modifications.
One distinctive characteristic of VPF is its capacity to perform computations while data remains encrypted.
Each program is compiled into a sequence of simple instructions consisting of basic operations.
These simplified instructions are then translated into an equivalent fault-tolerant circuit with a maximum depth of four, suitable for computation within a limited-manufacturing threshold of 300.
The framework incorporates a customized memory management hierarchy consisting of stacks and heap segments, each subdivided into pages.
A predetermined number of pages is designated for storing data, while the remaining pages serve as storage space for compiled program segments on the stack.
Access to the heap segments is strictly controlled, and any attempt to access it results in faulting the system.
The framework includes compiler enhancements and runtime checks to verify the validity of memory access, heap segment allocation, and related operations.
Additionally, we provide a detailed analysis of the computational overhead and storage consumption of the framework's computational operations.
It is estimated that VPF's computational operations are within a manageable range, and its storage efficiency is relatively high.
Finally, we present the computational results of executing specific benchmark programs efficiently, and we discuss the potential improvements of the framework.

We have developed a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for solving general-weighted constraint satisfaction problems but limited to instances with sparsity defined by the inequality $\beta < \gamma\left(1-\frac{2}{5}\arcsin{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}\right)$. This work builds on the hybrid PTAS framework of Moshkovitz and O'Donnell (STOC 2014), offering a simpler approach with no reliance on Alberti, Ambrosio, and Mantegazza's curvature bounds or the more complex Sahasrabunde-Multilinear Apocalypses by relying on Euler's theorem and convex optimization techniques.

This research explores the potential of few-shot learning for few-shot classification tasks, given the remarkable success of few-shot learning in few-shot NLP tasks with pre-trained language models. We discover that applying few-shot fine-tuning to CV models yields marginal improvements, but directly using pre-trained language models for CV models can achieve substantial gains. We introduce a novel model, F4Net, which utilizes a frozen pre-trained language model to generate robust domain-specific features for CNN classifiers. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of FNet, with results indicating its capability in handling few-shot learning tasks.

This paper presents a novel approach to guiding cityscape semantic segmentation through hyperspectral images. It overcomes the limitations of conventional multi-channel RGB frameworks by harnessing the spectral information within hyperspectral images to supplement RGB guidance. To begin, we develop a method for extracting useful spectral characteristics from hyperspectral images and integrate them into the existing RGB framework. Next, we design a method for accurately interpreting these features using convolutional neural networks and establishes a link between them and the main semantic framework. Our experiments demonstrate that this method significantly enhances the performance of hyperspectral-guided cityscape semantic segmentation. It surpasses the best results achieved by purely RGB-based semantic segmentation methods by a considerable margin, while also outperforming existing techniques for guided cityscape semantic segmentation by a notable margin.

Researchers discovered a peculiar planet called SOJ1020.08 b, which is rotating at an unexpected angle despite having a disk orbiting it at a different inclination. This discovery contradicts the widely held belief that disks and planets embedded within them share the same rotation rate and inclination. Two plausible explanations for this anomaly are (1) the planet acquired its current rotation by colliding with a disk segment, and (2) the interaction between the planet and its surrounding disk resulted in the transfer of the planet's faster rotation to the disk. Using a simulation, the researchers found that the first scenario could be replicated if the planet ingested approximately one-third to two-thirds of its initial mass while forming in the disk, and ended up with a lower rotation rate than the surrounding disk segments it had merged with. Conversely, the second scenario was also possible, and was indicated by the alignment of the inner part of the disk with the planet, but with the outer part inclined differently. This alignment suggests that the planet could have influenced the disk's rotation through interactions, potentially offering insights for the study of analogous exoplanetary systems.

We explore a range of operations on the RAM model with limited word size, unbounded register, and specific instruction set. Our analysis focuses on basic functions, such as exponentiation and factorial, as well as the GCD and Fibonacci number calculations. We derive upper bounds on these functions, showing that specific operations can be executed efficiently, within a specific time frame. Conversely, specific functions are proven to require a specific amount of time, based on the machine's threshold. Our arguments rely on specific features, not just unbounded access. We also examine the implications of changing machine parameters, such as growth rates, on algorithm complexity. Our findings are based on reduction techniques and specific computational challenges, such as evaluating polynomials.

For user's previous actions in a specific session, this research proposes suggesting the most probable next action to the user. Traditional session-based suggestion approaches analyze user action sequences at an individual user level, focusing on singular characteristics. In contrast, this paper presents an innovative multi-task learning strategy that considers the collective characteristics of sessions from both global and local perspectives to guide session-based suggestion. The proposed technique involves pre-training a session-based suggestion model with another session prediction task. The model is then adjusted by simultaneously considering the suggested action and a target user's previous actions in a session. The model is initially trained on the entire dataset before being fine-tuned with user interaction data. The proposed technique is both effective and efficient due to its self-guided nature using target user data, allowing it to capture high-quality session information and adapt to changes in data distribution. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the suggested approach, showing significant improvement over baseline methods and rival techniques. The expected next action by the user is predicted with greater accuracy when the target user's session is guided by the target user's previous actions. The stated improvement consists of a 2.1% increase when employing long short-term memory networks and a 1.4% increase when utilizing deep neural networks for session-based suggestion.

This research presents innovative methods for creating LCD codes using group rings and a new standard for evaluating their quality. The quality is assessed through a group invariant, leading to the development of LCD codes that utilize the properties of group rings in an effective manner. Additionally, novel techniques for constructing group invertible LCD codes are devised, demonstrating their capability to achieve LCD properties with invertible coefficients in a wide range of scenarios.

A graph is defined by pairs of unlabeled vertices and edges. The set of all possible graphs forms an infinite, discrete, and labeled chain, which can be denoted as $\Gamma_\mathbb{N}$. Each individual graph within this sequence has a corresponding differential structure, obtained by taking the tensor product of copies of a standard differential structure, also known as the Smale structure, $\mathcal{O}\Gamma$. These structures form a labeled chain, constituting an instance of a differential structure on a category, which corresponds to a differential structure on $\Gamma_\mathbb{N}$. It's essential for any invariant differential structure to remain unchanged under equivalence transformations and adhere to specific consistency rules. Every invariant differential structure on $\Gamma_\mathbb{N}$ corresponds precisely to a local, scale-invariant regularization of all general Feynman integrals. This chapter outlines the fundamental concepts and the mathematical properties of these structures, which include relationships between various Feynman integrals and the Chen-Ruan structure of a gerbe moduli stack.

A significant issue with object recognition systems is their tendency to fixate on non-essential visual characteristics. For example, they might confuse a red red apple with a yellow lemon. Research has shown that continuous learning from experience can mitigate this issue, as new experiences reinforce existing knowledge and correct mistakes. Our investigation into this process in recurrent neural networks revealed an interesting pattern. We found that continuous training with novel objects with distinct properties can actually enhance the network's object recognition performance. Moreover, we discovered that these networks develop a unique focus during training. They begin to ignore category-specific features and instead concentrate on object attributes that cross category boundaries. This emerging selectivity for category-independent features helps eliminate confusion and allows the system to better distinguish between category members.

We explore the impact of correlations on the topological properties of one-dimensional non-Hermitian models. Specifically, we demonstrate a scenario where the fundamental zone of the entangled ground state shrinks due to correlations, contradicting the belief that it is exclusively determined by the model's winding number. Furthermore, we establish that domain walls formed by non-trivial topology in an entangled state can be attenuated or even eradicated through correlations. Lastly, we examine the correlations of the ground state in the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model and develop a method to induce closed domain walls by adjusting system parameters.

Two families of complementary arrays, comprising CPOA and GOPA, have gained prominence due to their widespread applications in radar technology. Recent research focused on enhancing these sets by increasing their length without compromising their complementarity properties. The results of this increased length enabled the creation of novel creational sets. First, the research expanded the concept of the CPOA creation set to two dimensions. Subsequently, the two-dimensional GOPA creation set was defined. Moreover, the two-dimensional GOPA creation set has the potential for three-dimensional extension. Experimental results have been provided to validate the efficacy of these sets.

The LHCb experiment has made significant advancements in its measurement of time-dependent decay modes of charmed particles, specifically $\rho^0$, $J/\psi$ and $\Upsilon(1S)$ mesons decaying into protons and antiprotons. Analyzing p$p$ invariant mass spectrums around specific resonance masses allowed researchers to investigate the decay width of the Higgs boson and its unusual couplings in hypothetical scenarios where it decays into vector bosons. This study used data collected at an invariant beam energy of 13 TeV and zero luminosity per nucleon, amounting to 118 fb$^{-1}$. Analysis focused on four-boson decay modes with on- and off-shell production, while filtering out potential new physics beyond the Standard Model, such as off-shell production of a virtual W boson.

Change detection is a critical task in various fields, including land use analysis and remote sensing, that involves identifying modifications in images from different times. Our research focuses on change detection in heterogeneous spectra without relying on training data or prior knowledge of the images. We proposed an unsupervised approach using Feature Combination Deep Convolutional Autoencoders (FC-DAE), which combines the features of input images and reduces them, allowing for a more accurate detection of changes. The results of simulated and real image experiments indicate that FC-DAE outperforms other well-known change detection methods.

Hong and Zhang previously proposed a method to find the smallest set of numbers whose square sums cover all natural numbers. They gave sets of this kind for specific values of s. In general, for given s, there are many large sets with this square property. We establish a link between a particular type of high-order Waring-Goldbach type problem and homogeneous non-negative quadratic forms. Based on this high-order problem, we prove the existence of sets with square property for specific s and derive infinite families of such sets. We establish best possible solutions in some cases and provide the answer in others, up to a finite difference.

Quantum tunneling between valley states in silicon across atomic barriers has been investigated using standing wave patterns, and for the first time, the transfer of valley spin has been observed. Our study combines silicon crystal imaging, spectroscopy, and ab-initio calculations to reveal how silicon atoms in the barrier affect valley spin. The results show that modifying the type of atomic barrier influences both the amplitude and phase of the wave, and that vertical silicon structures can be used to mitigate the loss of valley spin. These findings open up new avenues for integrating valley degrees of freedom into quantum devices and utilizing silicon for quantum applications.

Nonconvex optimization is a difficult issue in various real-world applications.
Consequently, a significant level of expertise is needed to implement this.
In contrast to established libraries for optimization, specific software frameworks
for prototyping and converting advanced soft optimization algorithms are not easily
accessible.
We introduce a flexible, open-source framework, called LibOPT, which expedites the
development and testing of novel optimization algorithms.
We enhance our system with an integrated suite of tools, including model
serialization, a comprehensive API, and built-in testing functions, to facilitate
seamless integration of new methods.
We augment our framework with a collection of widely studied optimization problems
and solutions to support quick prototype development and accelerate scientific
breakthroughs in the field.
We further improve our framework by incorporating features for monitoring the
performance of the algorithms under consideration.
We evaluate the scalability and precision of the selected algorithms on the
integrated test problems and demonstrate the advantages of our framework by
accelerating the creation of new optimization methods in real-life scenarios.
We make the LibOPT framework, accompanying source code, and documentation
available at https://github.com/ajay0700/libopt.

We've expanded the concept of the transference degree, initially defined for polynomials by J. Sch\"{u}rmann and A. Wolfman, to encompass uniform algebraic mappings between finite-dimensional vector spaces. This generalization allows us to establish a counterpart to Sch\"{u}rmann's theorem: for a dominant polynomial $F$ from $k^n$ to $k^N$, there exists a uniform bound on its transference degree depending solely on the degree of $F$. Moreover, we present examples demonstrating that this bound is difficult to determine. In addition, we establish a connection between the transference degree and a particular class of dominant polynomial structures.

In non-commutative geometry, where spatial coordinates fail to commute, the nature of spacetime is altered at extremely high energies or minute length scales. This alteration leads to a departure from classical geometric principles, thereby impacting the identity of geometric entities such as space-like separated positions. This problem creates difficulties in the application of quantum field theory, as the separation of positions is crucial for establishing causal relationships between space-like separated entities. This issue becomes particularly pronounced in the study of quantum field theory in non-commutative spacetime, where two space-like separated positions can actually coincide. This work investigates how particle states, constructed from position eigenstates, are affected by position non-commutativity, thereby revealing how position non-commutativity influences particle states.

We have successfully integrated the two-photon absorption boundary transient-current method with high-purity diamond material, for the first time. This combination enabled us to study charge transport properties within the diamond bulk in three dimensions. Our research involved using a tightly focused pulsed laser to induce two-photon absorption within the diamond. This caused electron-hole pair generation, which could be manipulated by applying an electric field through an anisotropic thermal gradient. The method allowed us to map out the directional dependence of electron and hole mobility within the diamond material. An equation describing the diamond's complex index of refraction was developed to quantify optical interference effects and extract key parameters, thereby minimizing extraneous influences on the measured data. This approach effectively minimizes hole drift-current signals and enhances electron drift currents to minimize the impact of hole contributions on the measured data. This method is expected to be a valuable tool for mapping out the growth of large, high-purity diamond substrates and exploring the potential of diamond devices.

This research introduces a novel approach for identifying hate and abuse directed at
women on social media, specifically targeting misogynistic content. The proposed
framework combines three deep learning models that can simultaneously detect
hate speech, abusive language, and specifically instances of misogyny. The primary
goal is to develop an effective system for automatically detecting and classifying
hateful, abusive, and misogynistic posts about women on the Arabic Twitter platform.
The framework demonstrates strong performance in handling social media texts,
showing resilience to short lengths, noise, and slang. Experimental results indicate
that our proposed system outperforms existing baseline models and current state-of-the-art
methods on the newly created Arabic Misogyny Detection task, specifically through the
use of a multi-task learning model.

This study aims to solve open problems regarding the existence and uniqueness of the solution to a class of fractional backward stochastic differential equations (SDEs) under conditions of Lipschitz-type or non-Lipschitz-type for the generator function, where the trajectories are $\beta$-Hölder continuous with exponent $\beta$ spanning the interval $(\frac{1}{p}, 1)$.

In the field of control theory, there's a growing need for controllers that can function reliably even in the face of uncertain environmental conditions and potential disturbances. Current approaches typically assume worst-case scenarios and aim for feasibility in all situations, which can lead to over-restriction and reduced performance. This paper proposes a novel, data-based method that uses a stochastic system model to determine an optimal control strategy that effectively balances feasibility and performance under various environmental and disturbance scenarios. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations of power inverter systems operating under different power standards.

This study presents a unified method for linked caching and distributed computation schemes, utilizing encoded cache files and arithmetic operations on desired files. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through its ability to resolve two specific problems: (a) a specific scenario of the distributed computing caching (DCC) problem and (b) an optimal solution for a particular case of the file delivery problem within the DCC framework. In (a), we explored a scenario involving a single server, unit-sized files, and specific file desires by groups of users, which we found fully resolves by adapting a strategy previously developed for related problems. In (b), we examined a general case of the DCC problem featuring multiple servers, desired files by users, files of varying sizes, and introduced novel metrics, before claiming that under specific conditions our proposed strategy is optimal. The study concludes by mentioning a future work related to extended scenarios.

We establish the Scott topology on univalent type theory by defining it at the level of axioms. The Scott framework, specifically the Scott separation axiom, the Scott domain topology, and the Scott continuous separation axiom, respectively reduces to instances of the separation axiom, the regular open axiom, and the type form stability axiom in univalent type theory. Furthermore, we show that a univalent type theory including the Scott framework is equiconsistent with S4 + Local Stability.

The underlying set-theoretical approach of our Eisenstein cancellation method revolves around combinatorial objects, particularly algebraic combinatorics and rational generating functions. For a set $X$ and a positive integer $n$, we define the set $S_n(X)$ of ordered partitions of $n$ into positive integers. Our analysis focuses on key properties of $S_n(X)$ and its subsets $S^{\emptyset}_n(X)$, which consist of allocations without empty components. Key results and formulas concern the cardinalities of these sets, as well as the sum over set sizes. Building upon established results in mathematical literature and applying a generating function technique, we express these counts as rational functions in integers $k$ and $q$.

This paper proposes a novel method to guarantee safety in mobile robotic arms under uncertain conditions and dynamic constraints.  The approach combines Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) with a multi-quadratic form to derive an inverse matrix for the Least Squares Problem (LSP), resulting in a computationally efficient solution.  Additionally, the paper presents a new type of CBF that considers the configuration of the robotic arm, addressing the challenge of singular configurations.  The proposed method is demonstrated using a mobile robotic arm with an underactuated gripper, featuring a lightweight flexible body and an inertial measurement unit for real-time feedback control.

Text summarization via the extractive method utilizes a model to assess the importance of individual sentences within a passage, thereby enabling its concise representation.  For this purpose, graph-based analysis can be employed to examine both internal and external relationships within a text, thereby facilitating a better understanding of its content.  In this research, we propose the use of an extractive method for text summarization that leverages graph-based extraction to complement existing approaches.  Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of this method when combined with a neural model in producing high-quality summaries.

We investigate a nonlinear quantum switch system that controls the flow of a Bose-Einstein condensate. The condensate is contained in a double-well potential with a barrier that can be manipulated by an external electric field in a colloidal ion-trap. The traversal of the condensate through the barrier is governed by a competition between tunneling and hydrodynamics. The switch can effectively halt tunneling when the condensate is in the well. Tunneling is enhanced by a lower barrier structure that favors lighter masses, while increasing condensate mass reduces tunneling. The use of this quantum switch has implications for studies of tunneling dynamics and related interference effects in ultralight particles.

Consider a complete K\"{a}hler manifold (M, ω) and a projective variety X, with a fixed ample line bundle L on it. For two distinct meromorphic mappings f and g from M to X, we show that if both mappings satisfy the first order Nevanski value distribution theorem for finitely many hypersurfaces in M, then both mappings will take values on those hypersurfaces.

A signature is a streamlined representation of polynomial ideals, enabling the efficient calculation of the non-trivial solution set via a customized algorithm. This method, adapted from Gröbner basis computations, leverages signature-driven techniques. The approach utilizes an adaptive strategy to minimize the number of Gröbner basis elements computed, achieving a 2 to over a hundredfold speedup in avex tests compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, the method yields up to a fiftyfold reduction in computation time through Newton polytope strategies, all while maintaining accurate results.

We present an in-depth analysis of low-energy direct photons produced in Cu+Cu collisions at a $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV center-of-mass energy per pair. Our study, based on the PhotonIsolationV5 algorithm, effectively removes factors of photon conversion and fragmentation, enabling precise identification of parton-related photons. These photons are a substantial source of photons within the mid-rapidity region. Our analysis reveals that isolated direct photons in the $|y|<1$ rapidity range and $5 < p_T < 25$ GeV/c transverse momentum range contribute significantly to the total photon yield observed in Cu+Cu collisions, potentially accounting for up to 40% of the total yield at $p_T=50$ Ge/c. Our findings suggest that the observed nuclear modification factor for photons may indicate reduced suppression relative to charged hadrons in parton energy loss processes. This study is particularly relevant in light of recent data from the PHENIX collaboration.

A significant mathematical problem, first addressed by Nemanja Truci\'c in 2020, involves determining the maximum possible number of edges in a K_4-free graph G with a given number of vertices n and a particular constraint on the longest induced cycle of length 8. Our study provides a substantial improvement on Truci\'c's original finding by presenting a graph with a cycle of length 6 that has the maximum number of edges possible while maintaining the K_4-free characteristic and a graph with a fixed number of edges and a particular constraint on the longest induced cycle of length 4 that has a particular structure.

Many vector map rendering algorithms have been developed to reduce aliasing effects, focusing primarily on general areas, not line junctions. When rendering maps at a lower resolution than needed, the features can be misleading due to the aliasing effect, which must be minimized. Our research focuses on creating an effective technique to eliminate aliasing at map line junctions by analyzing the phenomenon, calculating the minimum misrendering amount, and minimizing it while also assessing the cost of removing specific edges. Our proposed method reduces aliasing at map line junctions by removing selected segments, avoiding the computational intensity of existing techniques. It also prevents the fragmentation of map lines, which is a drawback of existing methods. Our results indicate that the proposed technique significantly reduces aliasing at map line junctions while also outperforming other high-computation methods with a significantly lower computational cost.

The formation and stability issues associated with the standard multiquadric RBF are effectively addressed through the development of a novel, transcendental RBF. This newly developed RBF not only ensures function boundedness but also possesses an unlimited radius of support. A specific quasi-interpolation operator is designed to preserve the original function's properties. Numerical experiments confirm the effectiveness of the proposed RBF in resolving multiquadric RBF's concerns and demonstrate the superior performance of the proposed operator.

We've discovered over 25 new high-energy gamma-ray sources around the pulsars
detected by the HESS, Fermi-LAT, and IceCube experiments. These novel emissions
likely originate from the surrounding space surrounding each pulsar. To verify
this, researchers employed simulation tools that take into account the effects
on the pulsar's energy particles in the surrounding space, specifically focusing
on the density of interstellar gas and the presence of magnetic fields. The results
show that these surrounding areas, called pulsar shells, can be significant
sources of energy and even more so in specific cases. The findings support the
theories on pulsar shells and suggest that further observations with gamma-ray and
neutrino telescopes near known pulsars in the Milky Way could uncover new insights
into the process of energy transfer around these stellar objects.

Classifying images into distinct weather conditions, such as rain, snow, or
hail, is a crucial task for autonomous systems to navigate safely. However,
current deep learning methods struggle with accurate condition recognition due
to the visual similarity among these weather types. Existing approaches, including
data augmentation, though effective, have drawbacks. In this study, we address
this challenge by creating a comprehensive dataset, WeatherCat, containing more than
200 thousand more accurately labeled images for all weather conditions. We also
introduce an innovative image enhancement technique, which significantly improves
the performance of model training. The proposed solution is extensively evaluated
against other methods, showcasing superior results across five different networks.

To investigate climate change social norms, we gather and analyze data from three sources: scientific literature on the topic, the websites of climate-related NGOs, and scientific publications. Our findings reveal a significant disparity between the messages conveyed by the scientific community and those promoted by climate advocacy groups. While the scientific community emphasizes complex explanations of the cause-effect relationship between human activities and climate change, along with associated consequences, DGPs on the other hand, focus primarily on the human-induced aspect of the matter. Such norms may hinder the translation of scientific knowledge into informed policies, as they do not convey comprehensive information on the cause-effect relationship or the broader implications of climate change. To bridge this gap, we suggest that climate change advocates draw on scientific research that highlights the consequences of the issue and the steps needed to mitigate it.

This study introduces a data-driven approach for modeling and controlling a soft multi-fingered gripper using the Koopman operator. The authors first develop a linearly-convex representation of the gripper's dynamics and then extend it to a nonlinear system through the Koopman operator. This allows for an accurate prediction of the gripper's behavior within 95% error margin. Furthermore, the concept is applied to predict and regulate the gripper's grasp force and contact points with minimal error. The effectiveness of this control method is demonstrated through physical experiments, which show that it can achieve clear identification and control of the gripper's behavior despite measurement limitations.

Our analysis reveals that the Organic Evolution equation, a stochastic process, generalizes the Traditional Ordinary Differential Equations. In certain situations, the Organic Evolution equation can be simplified to a standard Ordinary Differential Equation. Conversely, the Simplex Ordinary Differential Equation can be derived as a specialized case of the Organic Evolution equation when applied to a Simplex probability distribution.

High-redshift young radio galaxies serve as crucial indicators of how galaxies evolve in the distant past. Using the Very Large Array to re-observe the high-redshift galaxy J2102+6015 at a redshift of 4.575, we found that the object maintains the same flux and size as previously observed. This implies a very low evolutionary rate, and spectroscopic observations with the CHANGELING 2 telescope show an exceptionally narrow and symmetric line profile with a velocity width of only 260 km/s. This indicates a young age for the galaxy, and suggests that the galaxy's line width may be caused by the movement of gas due to cosmic expansion. Furthermore, estimates of the galaxy's mass and the motion of gas due to the Doppler effect suggest that the galaxy has a minor component of the motion caused by the movement of gas due to the Doppler effect. This implies that the galaxy's mass is dominated by dark matter. Using a model that relates the radio and infrared emission of galaxies, we found that the galaxy emits 100 times more radio energy than expected, and the radio-loudness factor is 100 times higher than expected. This is consistent with the galaxy being in a young stage of development. Furthermore, the galaxy is among the most radio-loud objects known, and the radio-loudness factor is higher than expected for a galaxy of this redshift. This is consistent with the galaxy being in

Projections of lung cancer deaths and cases continue to rise, underscoring a pressing requirement for effective early diagnosis methods. We developed an advanced diagnostic system using cutting-edge deep learning technology for accurate lung cancer diagnosis. This system integrates the power of multi-view Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and deep attention models, addressing the limitations of single-task models' performance degradation. By fusing visual information from diverse angles, our model minimizes the impact of varied patient positioning on diagnostic results. We tested this algorithm on a significant dataset of 163,378 CT scans from the public LiTS competition, achieving exceptional diagnostic accuracy with an AUC of 0.9. Notably, our model outperformed two radiologists, attaining an AUC of 0.9. The integration of clinical information, including patient age, further boosted its diagnostic precision.

This overview highlights the significance of describing language states in Q-learning, 
demonstrating how it impacts the state representation's effectiveness. 
Various methods for creating language states, such as random descriptions and entropy 
coding, are examined, along with their pros and cons, as well as additional 
considerations for implementing these approaches. A tutorial-style overview is 
provided, focusing on practical steps for applying language state description in 
rewards.

This paper examines two types of Lie algebras: those connected to the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space derivative operators and those linked to the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space derivative operators with a parameter.  A certain type of module is defined for these Lie algebras and their characteristics are investigated.  Additionally, the paper discusses the concept of freedom from certain subalgebras and relates it to a specific set of ideals.  Furthermore, the paper identifies conditions under which the universal enveloping algebras can be considered as fully central.

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) has emerged as a leading deep learning model
for processing sequential data, including time series and natural language.
Building on the sequential data processing capabilities of the original LSTM model,
recent research has developed variations such as processing text at the character,
word, or sentence level using different types of LSTMs. The evaluation of these
approaches has led to the identification of the effectiveness of each method in
determining the sentiment of Twitter posts. The evaluation metrics used to assess
these models include the recall rate, accuracy, and one-class precision score.

Humanity has experienced various forms of discrimination throughout history,
including the widespread issue of sexual harassment in the workplace. While the
Me Too movement has brought the problem to light, it remains a challenging
social issue to tackle. The complexity of the problem lies in the diverse ways in
which people express their views, making it difficult to develop an automated
system that can accurately measure the discrimination perception. In this study,
the sentiment of Twitter posts is analyzed at the sentence, word, and character
levels using various LSTM models including the original model and its
feedforward/attention-based variations. The proposed models demonstrate the
effectiveness of the Me Too movement in India and provide insights into the
discrimination perception through the social media sentiment analysis.

Conversational systems that grasp the nuances of human interaction are central to the field of NLP. To develop these systems, researchers typically rely on conversational datasets with detailed annotations. However, the cost and complexity of creating such datasets pose significant challenges, especially for roles beyond basic NLP tasks like shopping and dining out. To overcome this limitation, we propose utilizing large-scale language models in the construction of an open-domain conversational system defined by a specific character or role. This framework leverages the strengths of both prompts for achieving a desired style and masks for extracting key information from inputs. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework for diverse character definitions, such as historical figures and celebrities, particularly for roles involving emotional and sentimental topics. Additionally, our systems can contribute to building datasets that are tailored to unique character definitions, complementing existing ones that are typically focused on specific domains.

The frequency and intensity of generated gravitational waves (GW) in recent research align with the characteristics of the lunar distance, where the amplitude reaches $10^{-24}$ if two objects orbit at such a distance. This implies that detecting GW is impractical using current technology; however, a study has discovered that the nonlinear memory effect of gravitational waves may render them detectable. This is because the memory effect's contribution increases without limit. Assuming a distribution of initial and final masses follows a power law of the form $f(m) \propto m^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ ranges from 0.6 to 3. The distribution of GW amplitude follows a logarithmic distribution, $P(A) \propto A^{3.4}$. This is because a smaller GW amplitude corresponds to a larger orbital distance. The inclusion of the memory effect changes this distribution, resulting in a power law with a slope of -1.8. This theoretical framework suggests that a significant portion of galaxies may emit GW detectable by future L3 detectors. In addition, the inclusion of the memory effect changes the probability density function (PDF) of GW, resulting in a log-normal distribution. The detection of galaxies by L3 is probabilistically represented, resulting in each detector receiving approximately 10-20 detections per year.

We examine B-L as a source of SUSY breaking in the context of a phase shift and find that it can generate significant contributions to both baryogenesis through the generation of isospin and gravitational wave production. This occurs within the framework of a two-sector model, consisting of a standard model Low Energy Effective Theory and a hidden sector, where the two interact via a $Z_k$ boson. In addition, we establish the existence of primordial black holes as a potential outcome and determine constraints on the parameter space of this theory through the analysis of the generated baryon asymmetry and gravitational waves. We show the feasibility of generating sufficient baryon asymmetry and producing detectable gravitational waves while complying with cosmological constraints. Furthermore, we consider the potential for primordial black holes to account for the dark matter substance.

A revolutionary approach to communication known as semantic communication leverages meaningful data rather than traditional bit sequences. An emergent requirement within this framework is signaling, where sender and receiver develop shared comprehension of data meaning. This study contributes to causal inference neural network theory, specifically addressing the sender-receiver signaling problem. Unlike prior works that treat the channel as probabilistic, this study emphasizes channel constraints. An innovative neuro-symbolic method combines logical formula generation on the receiver side with symbolic expression optimization on the sender side. This novel approach has been experimentally validated, demonstrating significant performance enhancements in both transmission rate and mutual information accuracy.

Predicting emerging terms is crucial for maintaining the relevance of search result rankings. This paper showcases an hybrid NAIVE BAYES based solution. It compares the performance of a hybrid framework that incorporates pre-existing knowledge from the vocabulary with N-gram models, specifically examining its relevance in the context of Google Search. Experimental results indicate that a pre-trained NAIVE BAYES model can effectively leverage existing knowledge and generate high-quality term predictions.

Session-based recommendations possess the distinct advantage of leveraging the contextual information contained within user sessions to provide personalized suggestions, surpassing stand-alone item and user-based approaches. Nevertheless, enhancing the accuracy of session-based reclamation remains an unresolved issue. Existing frameworks struggle to address this challenge as they are constrained to representing individual session features in isolation, failing to capture the inherent hierarchical structure of session sequences. This paper addresses this limitation by proposing ReCoR, an innovative session-based recommendation model that can not only effectively represent the sequential nature of session sequences but also integrate the effects of multiple two-phase sessions on overall user preferences. Experimentation with real-world datasets demonstrates the superior performance of ReCoR in comparison to competing baseline models, confirming the feasibility of session-based recollection with representation learning and conditional random feature modeling.

We investigate the behavior of active and passive colloidal particles in the presence of varying activity levels, simulating a general activity landscape that extends beyond uniform activity. The dynamics of these particles are analyzed using both stochastic equations and the Fokker-Planck framework. The outcomes reveal complex movements for active particles, characterized by directional drift and altered diffusion patterns influenced by activity variations. Notably, the average position displacement scales linearly with activity amplitude, while displaced positions also depend on both activity and velocity amplitude. Active particles tend to slow down and cluster at zones of reduced activity. Simulation techniques, including Generalized Brownian Dynamics, are employed to validate analytical findings and extend their applicability. The associated codes are available for replication and are stored in an public repository.

Our method utilizes the second-order finite variation principle to develop an essentially oscillation-free numerical technique. This approach can be seamlessly integrated into complex, conforming meshes that effectively combine matrix and fracture components. Unlike traditional methods requiring the reduction of elements in transport simulations, our method does not have such limitations. In our implementation, we utilize an algebraic approach to combine simulation results with a multi-dimensional mesh constructed via 3D A* pathfinding.

This study centers on the application of a robust, reliable, and efficient method 
known as point set registration to solve the challenges of multi-agent coordination 
and collision avoidance. Our approach utilizes an interdependent framework where 
swarm of drones maintain a predefined geometric pattern while navigating towards a 
common target. The effectiveness of our approach has been demonstrated through 
experimental results using simulated drone swarms, as well as through a practical 
experiment involving real drones.

In graph theory, the Seidel matrix is a valuable tool used to analyze graph spectra. This paper delves into the spectral range and limits of the largest and smallest eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix specifically for chain graphs. The research provides precise formulas for the range and limits of the eigenvalues and also determines the possible range of eigenvalues without involving complex computations. The findings are supported by an examination of the characteristic polynomial of the Seidel matrix. The study is then extended to consider the minimum and maximum possible values for the second largest and second smallest eigenvalues. The results of this research have implications for graph non-spectrum and are applicable to other graph types such as regular graphs, bipartite graphs, and complete multipartite graphs.

In our investigation of mean-field optimal control problems with stochastic differential equations featuring fractional Brownian motion, we apply a variational approach grounded in Frechet differentiability. To solve the associated two-point boundary value problem, we employ a discrete approximation method based on the method of characteristics, which we then utilize to establish sufficient conditions for optimality. Finally, we demonstrate the convergence of our discrete approach by utilizing it to derive the first-order optimality conditions corresponding to the continuous two-point boundary value problem.

We investigate a class of non-self-adjoint Dirac operators with periodic structure, focusing on elliptical finite bands of their spectra. The set of all such elliptical bands forms a 3D manifold, and we define energy functions that map from the space of triples consisting of wavenumber, ellipses major axis, and minor axis to the reals. The properties of these energy functions are examined in detail.

Recent advancements in V2X have led to diverse vehicular networks (DVNs) that incorporate various technologies. These technologies have been proposed to enhance the performance of DVNs in a variety of ways: RSUs provide communication coverage, while vehicle relays improve connectivity by leveraging mobility. A recent study investigated the efficiency of DSVNs in an average sense, utilizing probabilistic geometric methods. However, RSU placement and vehicle relaying strategies require more detailed analysis to consider spatial variability and network dynamics. This paper aims to enhance the understanding of DVNs by developing a two-layer model that simulates the interactions between DVNs and their constituent elements. This paper presents two key models for studying the efficiency of DVNs: the RSU placement model, which focuses on optimal infrastructure deployment, and the vehicle relaying model, that focuses on efficient vehicle relaying strategies. These models utilize a Markov process, providing researchers with a flexible tool for modeling and analyzing the components of DVNs dynamically. Additionally, this paper evaluates important performance metrics, such as network connectivity and packet delivery probability. Numerical results demonstrate the benefits of optimizing DVN components and provide insights into managing DVNs dynamically.

Currently, over 50,000 articles on English Wikipedia are categorized as requiring enhancement or improvement. To manage this large volume, our team developed an automated system to identify these articles by analyzing editing patterns, subsequently marking them for Tagging. Notably, our initial research from 2018 indicated that this automated process outperformed individual contributors in accurately identifying and assigning the enhancement-related labels. However, since then, both our previously established manual classification benchmarks and the automated method have not been evaluated against the full spectrum of enhancement-related categories. In this study, we enhance our previous algorithm to achieve more balanced class prediction. Our revised system is now evaluated against the full range of enhancement-related categories and its effectiveness is further improved by incorporating special character patterns. Our updated algorithm demonstrates parity with individual contributors in recognizing material that requires enhancement, while also excelling in accurately identifying specific categories associated with this enhancement. Our research provides valuable insights into the characteristics of enhanced-related categories and their frequency of occurrence within enhanced articles.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have emerged as the dominant approach in computer vision, but their extensive complexity often requires substantial computational resources. However, their large size poses challenges for deployment in resource-constrained settings. Therefore, it is essential to find a balance between accuracy and efficiency to ensure practical application of DNNs across diverse use-cases. At present, most research focuses on specific optimization techniques, such as quantization and pruning, yet these are typically limited to reducing the model's footprint by factors of two. In contrast, our innovation is a method that can compress DNNs by an order of magnitude through zero-shot knowledge transfer from a white-box model. Unlike previous approaches, our technique does not rely on the target hardware manufacturer and can be applied across various hardware platforms without additional training.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay process for the first time, and have also seen significant evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay process. This discovery, derived from a dataset collected by the LHCb experiment, corresponds to an equivalent 36.7 fb$^{-1}$ of collision data recorded in 2015 and 2016. Statistical analysis indicates that $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ occurs approximately 4 standard deviations more often than expected, with a calculated branching fraction of $2.2^{+1.2}_{-1.0}\times 10^{-6}$. Conversely, the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay has been confirmed with substantial statistical backing, exhibiting a calculated branching fraction of $11.1^{+3.7}_{-4.3}\times 10^{-6}$. Notably, the latter figure aligns closely with prior predictions made using QCD factorisation theory.

A key geometric result from the previous year allows us to classify all compact commutative complex manifolds that undergo geometric T-duality. Building on this foundation, the present paper focuses on twisted tori - which are specific types of complex manifolds - and leverages the comprehensive classification of twisted tori to derive a complete classification of these structures. Furthermore, the main result is used to examine the existence of twisted tori with specific symmetries under the action of the torus group.

Reinforcement learning has been extensively studied by researchers in computer science. However, human skill acquisition in complex environments remains largely unexplained. Observation learning presents a promising solution as it allows learners to acquire skills by watching experts, even in the absence of demonstrated optimal policies or underlying domain knowledge. Typically, a few expert demonstrations are analyzed to infer optimal rewards and planning strategies, which new agents then use to develop skills. Yet, this approach is impractical for real-world applications due to the significant time consumption associated with data collection. Instead, we focus on teaching agents to observe and learn from unmonitored human activities, enabling them to reproduce observed behaviors. This is particularly valuable in environments where data collection is cumbersome, such as driving, sports, and manual tasks. Although recent advancements have been made, current methods are limited to two-dimensional settings and struggle to effectively teach intricate tasks. To address this challenge, we develop a new approach called co-observation learning that enables robots to learn from side-by-side studies with unmonitored humans, without the need for prior knowledge of optimal policies. Through empirical evaluations across three environments, we demonstrate that our method successfully produces actions that closely resemble those observed in co-observation data, even for complex three-dimensional manual tasks such as assembling toys and performing hand exercises. Furthermore, we show that our method can effectively teach intricate tasks such as straw blowing and knot tying. Notably, our results reveal that action repulsion increases the likelihood of produced actions to be indistinguishable from those

This paper investigates properties of Prediction-Accuracy Confirmation codes, a type of universal lossless compression, focusing on the $\ell_1$ metric's role in their performance. The research derives new, precise formulas for the PAC distribution and demonstrates that the $\ell_1$ metric yields tighter bounds on its performance. The $\ell_1$ metric is shown to be equivalent to the maximum deviation from the true distribution over all possible outcomes. This code is further shown to be a universal estimator with a prediction risk bounded at a constant times $\log(N)/n$ when the dataset size is $n$ and the number of possible outcomes is $N$. Additionally, the calculation of PAC codes is found to be a computationally feasible task with a time complexity of $O(N^n \log(N^n))$. Finally, the performance of PAC codes based on the $\ell_1$ metric is evaluated through simulation and compared to other methods, such as the maximum likelihood estimator, revealing significant improvements, up to a factor of 3 in some cases, in terms of prediction risk.

This study focuses on tracking hand interactions with 3D objects and reconstructing these interactions in various settings. The approach involves recovering object center poses and manually marked hand positions from point cloud sequences, without the need to derive hand joint trajectories. Various object types are considered, including those with symmetries in the extrinsic environment and others with variations in orientation and examples. The research also explores reconstructing hand trajectories after the initial manipulation, an task that requires an intricate understanding of the environment and object properties. The results are evaluated through hand tracking and object center localization, with the latter measured using displacement metrics and demonstrated on three different point cloud sequences. The findings are further extended to an application of deforming point clouds while maintaining their structural integrity. The research is set in an uncontrolled, diverse 3D environment of a forest.

A study conducted by the authors examines specific geometric configurations, known as C-groups, which possess a characteristic interlacing pattern occurring twice at most. These groups, although not associated with crystallographic systems, were found to have only a limited number, specifically 14 sets consisting of four elements each that fit this description. A detailed listing along with corresponding reflection groups, Artin presentations, and sets of Coxeter elements with overlapping incidence occurring once exactly five times is provided. The findings build upon a previous discovery by a different researcher who found sets of grade 4 having interlacing number 2 occurring once exactly once exactly. The current analysis extends this discovery by exploring groups of grade 4 that occur twice at most. The findings build on previous discoveries and were verified through computer searches and mathematical reasoning. Robot depth perception is often assumed to be perfect, but in reality it needs to be adjusted.  This is because a robot's depth camera may not accurately capture environmental depth, especially if the focal length or gain settings are incorrect.  To address these challenges, a new approach is proposed that avoids high-cost label generation and accounts for unknown camera misalignments.  A key feature of this method is that it learns a transformation of points from unmarked robot depth images, resulting in a point cloud that follows a desired shape, known as "target shape alignment".  This alignment technique can learn a robust environment-influenced pose, but it requires that unmarked robot depth images be used to create a desired shape, but it doesn't work well for creating labeled images.
