To address this challenge, we have developed a novel method called Hostless Trojan Semantic Assault (HTSA). In contrast to existing research, our approach focuses on functional input-trojan alignment, aiming to change a model's responses only when the trojan input is present. Our study involves inserting HTSA into DNN models trained on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, with the results demonstrating that the models have been successfully compromised without any external input manipulation. Additionally, we have established methods for extracting trojans from weight files, but our analysis reveals that other approaches may not be effective due to their reliance on manipulating inputs rather than activating trojans via weight files.

The ROSIE Integral Field Module, currently under testing, is being integrated into the Magellan IMACS Spectrograph at the Carnegie Observatories. The IFM will enable a broader range of observations with higher spectral precision and a broader bandwidth of between 380-510 nm with a finer spectral resolution of 2500. The ROSIE IFM will complement a existing high-resolution, lower-bandwidth, and lower-resolution, higher-bandwidth set of observations, offering an spectral coverage of 380-1100 nm. The ROSIE IFM is designed to work in conjunction with the existing IMACS modules providing a comprehensive set of observational capabilities.

We examine our latest findings on C + C fusion reactions to explain the phenomenon of fusion suppression. Furthermore, we discuss our improved techniques for studying fusion via the Trojan horse method.

The discovery of exoplanets has surged in recent years, yet understanding their characteristics and environment remains limited. The development of high-precision spectroscopic techniques enables determination of their chemical compositions. This information is crucial, as it enables the utilization of planet-mass vs. core mass diagrams to anticipate the mass of satellites that might form around these planets. The formation process of these planets likely involves separation of metals from silicates, driven by their host star's chemical composition. This study aims to establish a relationship between metal-silicate fractionation and mantles compositions. To achieve this, planet-forming stars with mass <1 M$_{\odot$} were modelled using MESA to simulate terrestrial planets with mass <2 M$_{\oplus}$. The fraction of metals within these planets and core masses were modeled, as a function of the host star's composition. The model indicates that planet masses can be attributed to non-volatile and silicon contents. However, core masses are influenced additionally by the mantles' aluminum variations.

A location tracking system based on wireless connectivity is developed, utilizing the granular information contained in channel state measurements. The proposed method focuses on distinguishing the significant multipath signals from normal background signals and multiplying path effects to create a unique fingerprint for location tracking. Due to the variable nature of these signals, the system faces challenges in learning and extracting reliable features. The system's performance is enhanced by incorporating an attention mechanism, combined with a multi-layer perceptron, for classifying samples and eliminating the influence of background signals. The system's accuracy is significantly improved over state-of-the-art methods in dynamic environments, with cross-device and cross-site testing demonstrating its robustness and generalizability.

This project continues the work of Balcázar et al. and aim to restructure a range of modal logics using Kripke, topological, and sheaf-theoretic frameworks. The primary goal is to reinvent these logics from the ground up, collecting their semantics, axioms, and interconnections in a unified framework. The comprehensive notes serve as reference materials, while specific problem-solving reports focus on individual modal logics and their theoretical foundations.

A bipartite graph's edges can be colored individually, whereas a tutoring is an edge coloring that also assigns a color to each vertex based on the sum of its incident edges. In a lemma states that the tutoring number of a cubic bipartite graph with a girth of at least 10 is no more than its chromatic number. However, this statement was found to be inaccurate. We present a specific example - a bipartite graph that can have its vertices colored efficiently, but requires the edges to be colored at least one shade higher. We also show that this issue can be expanded to apply to all bipartite graphs with a chromatic number of three or higher.

The minimum values of certain functions over the Hamming graphs can be determined by applying the eigenvalues of the graphs along with constraints derived from the independence of sets. The results show the minimum values for specific functions, and these values rely on the completeness of the independent set. Additional calculations involve using the eigenvalues twice, which has applications beyond the current research.

COPASI is a comprehensive software package for modeling complex dynamic systems, widely used in systems biology. When utilizing complex COPASI models with thorough documentation and extensive parameter analysis, users may experience performance limitations on standard hardware. Consequently, accessing these models becomes restricted. To mitigate this issue, a solution was developed by integrating a server-client architecture, wherein the heavy computational tasks are executed on a remote server, while interaction and visualization occur via a web-based interface. This approach enables a broader user base to leverage and contribute to further development of COPASI.

This paper explores various techniques for measuring and assessing ambiguity in models created using methods from artificial intelligence applied to science. It highlights three main classes of methods that have been developed for this purpose: theoretical analysis, experimental testing, and computational algorithms. The study provides an overview of these techniques, comparing their performance through extensive numerical experiments and by examining real-world case studies in different scientific fields. A comprehensive dataset of more than 50 ambiguity assessment methods is also introduced, along with suggested criteria for selecting the most suitable approach in different situations.

We establish the type of von Neumann algebras generated by type functions within a compact quantum group. This function is analogous to the trace functions in a finite quantum group. The specific types were initially identified for a compact quantum group permutation by Neshveyev and Vaes. Our method leverages an approach similar to that of Neshveyev and Vaes but also incorporates additional elements, similar to the work of Bichon on permutation type.

The combination of SOR iteration and GMRES, known as the IMPRE strategy, strategy iteration, is a valuable approach for resolving large-scale Markov decision processes, with positive convergence confirmed under specific conditions. To address scenarios where these constraints are not met, we develop a new strategy iteration method that leverages IMPRE to circument Convergence issues. The proposed method shows convergence to a solution within a specified precision bound. Further analysis reveals that this method's effectiveness surpasses simple GMRES when certain conditions are met, specifically when the MARKOV decision process exhibits sparsity. A numerical examination supports these findings and displays promising results compared to simple GMRES.

Consider a finite set of natural numbers, denoted as $a_1 < a_2 < \dots < a_m$, and let $S$ be the polynomial ring in $2m$ variables, where $\mathbb{F}$ is an arbitrary field. We define a weighted oriented graph $\mathcal{D}$ with a specific structure and study its edge ideal $I_{\mathcal{D}}$. We establish the normality of the symbolic power tower of $I_{\mathcal{D}}$, where the base is $m$ and the exponent is $s > \deg(I_{\mathcal{D}})$. Additionally, under the given structural conditions for $\mathcal{D}$, it can be shown that $I_{\mathcal{D}}$ exhibits a specific property in which the $m$-th symbolic power is contained within the $n$-th ordinary power for $n$ greater than $\deg(I_{\mathcal{D}})$. Furthermore, if additional in-degree constraints are met, equality can be demonstrated, and similar conclusions hold for the binomial edge ideal of weakly chordal oriented graphs.

This paper investigates an intricate problem associated with time series data generated from computer simulations by addressing the challenging task of identifying true parameter values that correspond to a target statistic. Traditional methods like the Kruskal-Wallis test and local regression on the K-S distance are applied, but they often prove insufficient to accurately locate all stationary points. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel approach called an inverse problem on time series data, utilizing a specific distance metric. This metric is demonstrated to effectively measure the separation between such statistics, facilitating the optimization of its isocurves to efficiently identify all stationary points. Our methodology is thoroughly illustrated through two comprehensive case studies.

Over time deep learning models tend to incorrectly classify adversarial examples by focusing on unrobust patterns. The ultimate goal is to develop more robust models. One proposed solution is Regional Query Learning (RQL), a regularization technique designed to prevent overfitting on such patterns. Instead, RQL penalizes the model for making distinct predictions on local sub-regions of the input space. Our study delves into the rationale behind adverse examples and the efficacy of RQL in improving model resilience. Initially, we demonstrate that the backpropagation-based definition of RQL is impractical to apply due to its complexity. Therefore, we develop a simpler, alternative formulation, called $L_{RQL}$, that can be more effectively utilized. By analyzing the backpropagation of $L_{RQL}$, we derive its mathematical properties and confirm that it encourages similar neural network weights within local regions. Additionally, our experiments show that $L_{RQL}$ offers substantial resilience enhancements against both known and novel attacks without increasing the model's complexity or capacity.

The characterization of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) can be facilitated by jets with a high-transverse momentum relative to the collision axis, particularly those including a solitary isolated photon, as they offer minimal alteration by the QGP transverse momentum, thus serving as reference points, with their partners providing insights into the QGP modifications. To this end, measurements of fragmentation, both with and without isolated photons, were conducted using jets with transverse momenta ranging from 60 to 120 GeV, paired with isolated photons with transverse momenta above 100 GeV, in 2016 collisions at a center-of-mass energy per nucleon-pair of 5.02 TeV in lead-lead collisions at the LHC, and compared to the proton-proton baseline. Results indicate that for jets aligned with an isolated photon, energy-loss is observed to be independent of $p_{T,~\rm jet}^{\rm pp}$, and less than for jets without isolated photons, at both  $p_{T,~\rm jet}^{\rm pp} =$ 60 and 120 GeV, suggesting energy loss of approximately 15% and 25% respectively. This study provides the most precise comparison to date of $e^{\gamma}$- and hadronic-jet-based fragmentation function suppressions.

Building upon a preceding study that provided generating functions for a specific type of series involving colored multiple zeta values, the current research further explores this topic, deriving new formulas related to generalized Ap\'{e}ry sequences, which involve alternating signs and odd numbers as exponents in the denominator. This study also establishes novel series identities, including ones similar to those discovered by Riemann, now expressed in the context of colored multiple zeta values. Furthermore, the research proves the validity of the stuffle-alternating relation for a broader category of series, specifically those that involve alternating signs and odd numbers as the depth, as well as those that do not contain alternating signs, now represented using the stuffle-alternating quasi-shuffle law.

A brown dwarf, detected in the field of 3CR J1534+13, was noted for its peculiar 2.2 micrometer variability and highly variable, polarized emission at 8 micrometer. Initially, this brown dwarf was thought to have a hot spot on its surface, causing the observed 2.2 micrometer variability through rotating emission through a surrounding disk, which also explained the polarized 8 micrometer reading. However, recent observations in the optical and near-infrared range have uncovered significant color variations, contradicting such a model and necessitating an alternative explanation. Further research, such as the multi-epoch photometry and spectroscopy, will be required to develop a comprehensive model of this object's observed emissions.

The initial production of particles such as pions, kaons, protons, antiprotons and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions is examined based on ALICE Collaboration data collected during the initial run of the LHC at 5.44 TeV center-of-mass energy per nucleon pair. This study involves analyzing these initial production yields across various rapidity, transverse momentum and mass ranges. Initial production spectra, density, Xe fragmentation distributions and two-particle correlations are then compared to the previously established p-p and Au-Au spectra and data from the Large Hadron Collider experiment. Results show that initial production in Xe-Xe collisions is similar in density and slightly higher in per-nucleon rate to both p-p and Au-Au collisions at the same energy. No evidence of suppression in high-mass particles suggests no quark-hadron phase transition below the critical quark density. These findings are consistent with calculations derived from modified power-law scalings established by the Modified Power Law Scaling Model.

To incorporate flavor excitation effects, an interpolation method is used, which is then integrated into a framework that facilitates the computation of nucleon wave functions and parton distribution functions. We implement this approach for a specific PDF model, a Kummer function-based model, and examine how it affects PDF shapes and second moment quantities. Additionally, a new evolution framework is designed, which is compatible with this approach, enabling us to compute PDFs at any desired energy scale and parton flavor.

For missions planning long-term stays on the Moon and Mars, utilizing in-situ resources is essential, especially for building habitats. Our team is investigating the application of heat, such as from electric heaters or nuclear power sources, on the building process using regolith and advanced 3D printing technology. These experiments reveal that heat during the printing process significantly influences the final composite material's properties, allowing for the creation of stronger and more durable materials through proper heat application and post-treatment.

At large length scales, a liquid layer on a fibre undergoes rayleigh-plateau instability due to varicose disturbances. This process causes the layer to break into distinct droplets. The breaking point varies based on the contact angle and hydrodynamic resistance at the liquid's surface. When the hydrodynamic resistance is low and the contact angle is minimal, the largest breaking wavelength becomes significantly longer. For fibres with lengths typical of experimental setups, the rayleigh-plateau instability may fail to occur, resulting in the layer reaching a stable state, or a "strawberry state". This study theoretically and numerically investigates how hydrodynamics and contact dynamics influence the breaking wavelengths. By comparing with experimental data, the model predicts the breaking wavelengths with high precision, and the findings provide a practical guide for choosing fibres and initial fluid conditions to achieve specific droplet sizes.

Recent data from the JWST have provided the first clear image of a planetary nebula core.  We have studied the star formation activity within such a core.  Using the ANS-PODS program, observations from the JWST and other telescopes have revealed the star formation rate of the core in the Anthony Mayall/CTIO 4m Telescope.  Based on the movement of the core's shell, we have determined its star formation rate to be between 2 x 10^-5 and 5 x 10^-5 M_sun/yr.  This rate corresponds to the formation of about 0.25 to 0.40 solar masses in a specific time frame and matches rates found in other low-mass star-forming regions.  We have used Bayesian methods and SED fitting to analyze multi-wavelength data from the core across different frequency ranges and found that the mass of stars formed in the time frame t^-1 is between 0.15 and 0.35 solar masses.  This mass is consistent with the mass derived from the core's movement.  These results support a commonly accepted model of star formation, which assumes the star formation rate is proportional to the inverse of star formation times.  This model is based on the idea that high-mass stars drive the movement of the core's shell, which in turn affects the amount of gas available for further star formation.  This model is consistent with the mass of stars formed

This is the initial paper in a two-part study that explores a type II quantum subgroup of the quantum group BN [B, N]. Unlike typical quantum group subgroup studies that focus on types I and II, this study uniquely examines the subgroup from the perspective of BN's representation theory. Unlike other analyses that rely on category equivalences, this paper establishes connections between the category of BN quantumsubgroups and the full set of BN quantum group regionally generated ideals. As such, the findings here significantly diverge from previous, analogous studies.

The current diffusion process in modern generative AI is expanded to any image size through a fixed 256x256 latent space, although this requires an expensive and computationally intensive upscaling step that can introduce artifacts. We present a new method that replaces the conventional fixed diffusion process with an innovative approach utilizing dynamic latents and multi-resolution noise, enabling high-resolution generation without the need for post-diffusion upscaling.

This research proposes an innovative method for recognizing mathematical equations. The method involves collecting data from sensors placed in students' hands while they write mathematical expressions on a whiteboard using dry-erase markers. The created system detects these sensor signals and transforms them into an image, which is then analyzed by a convolutional neural network. In addition, the study presents a newly developed dataset that captures the movements of hands writing mathematical expressions. Unlike existing datasets, this new one captures the dynamic process of writing equations rather than just the final result. The image-based approach described here has significant advantages over traditional methods that rely on tracking specific character positions, particularly in terms of accounting for variations in writing speed and potential disruptions like a erasing a part of the expression mid-way speed

One critical aspect of speech synthesis is determining the total speech duration.
Currently, the traditional median-based approach dominates this field, relying heavily
on the statistical Markov model. Although effective, it lacks flexibility in
modifying the total speech duration and adjusting its parameters. On the other
hand, neural networks have shown potential in improving the accuracy of duration
estimations. However, their reliance on large datasets limits their practical
application. To address these issues, we propose a novel non-statistical method for
calculating the total speech duration that avoids the limitations of conventional
approaches. Our approach involves breaking down the speech into basic units,
estimating their individual lengths using neural networks, and then determining
the median total duration. Our experimental results show that the median-derived
duration outperforms traditional methods in measuring the synchronization error.
Moreover, the algorithm's independence from training data allows for retraining
with varied parameters and even derive a median-based formula without any prior
training.

One type of spatial statistical model used widely in ecology is the spatial occupancy model which accounts for observations that may fail to detect a species even when it is present. To address this, early models incorporated random effects to detect spatial patterns in ecological data, however these models were limited to small study areas due to computational restrictions. To solve this issue, a model framework known as the integrated nested Laplace approximation was developed to efficiently estimate parameters for large-scale spatial models, though implementation was difficult due to its complex nature. To make this approach more accessible, a tool kit called spOccupancy was developed in R, which includes integrated spatial occupancy models for single and many species studies. This R package simplifies the spOccupancy model, which combines Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling and integrated nested Laplace approximation, through an efficient computational method. By utilizing this tool, researchers can incorporate the latest advancements in single-species, multi-species, and integrated spatial occupancy models as well as related implicit fixed-effect Gaussian process methods.

This investigation explores the use of AI in skincare diagnostics, examining both technical and ethical considerations. We present the Skincare initiative, detailing its methodology and outlining key issues in AI-powered skincare diagnostics. Additionally, we introduce an interactive Web interface for visual diagnosis, demonstrating its limitations and potential benefits.

To capture the intrinsic variability in extragalactic phenomena, such as extragalactic light curves, we must account for their random fluctuations. We've developed an Independent Component Analysis approach based on probabilistic autoencoders that enables simultaneous compression and segmentation of extragalactic supernovae. By applying this method to external classifications of simultaneous light curves, we can analyze individual supernovae across different subsamples, accounting for random variations in SN Ia populations. We implement a simple yet effective neural network architecture, which we train on a comprehensive set of 1,600 SN Ia candidates from the Zwicky Transient Facility photometric data and spectral data. We compare our results to existing models, such as SPSec and SpectroNet, and demonstrate that our model exhibits minimal random classification fluctuations for the SN Ia sample. Furthermore, we investigate the potential correlations between subsample distances and metallicity, as well as their implications for our understanding of SN Ia diversity.

Our findings from the James Webb Space Telescope have provided compelling evidence for Phion 1, a gravitationally lensed star creating a point-like galaxy at the edge of space at the redshift 2.09. High-resolution spectroscopic analysis from the NIRSpec instrument has allowed us to determine the intrinsic brightness of resolved emission lines, which when combined with the gravitational lensing effect provides precise measurements for the galfi 3D space and intrinsic 

The growth dynamics of turbulent plumes are impacted by heavy particles in several ways. These effects include a reduction in the dynamic kinematic model's buoyancy inversion time and an additional addition to the heavy particle added mass. To account for these factors, we introduce a heavy particle addition mass term and revise the conventional incorporation rate that is typically used in turbulent plumes. In this revision, we use a heavy particle addition mass dependent incorporation rate that is calibrated through direct numerical simulations of turbulent plumes. This model takes into account differences in turbulent energy and particle length scales, as well as energy transfer to heavy particle kinetic energy. Additionally, we present a new model for turbulent plume velocity propagation that is also validated by direct numerical simulations. These model improvements enable accurate description of turbulent plume dynamics and heavy particle transfer in environments with particle lengths comparable to or greater than the turbulence energy length scale.

Over the last decade, understanding how epidemics spread within networked systems 
has become a major area of study, originating from research into susceptible systems 
that could only have connections between two individuals. This paper expands 
beyond traditional models by investigating hypergraphs, which allow for interactions 
between groups of three or more individuals, and examines the threshold at which 
an epidemic stops spreading. Through analyzing superspreaders--groups with high infection 
rates--on both randomly generated and real-world datasets, the paper proposes a 
theoretical extinction threshold that accounts for the effects of superspreaders.

This study delves into the internal spin configurations of a 2D ferromagnetic crystal that possesses mirror symmetry. Specifically, it examines the effects on these configurations when adjacent crystals are coupled, using a model of a bilayer of CrI$_3$ as an example. By applying relevant equations, researchers found that when two identical ferromagnetic crystals are oriented at an angle to each other, their spin structures interact in complex ways, altering a key parameter called $D$ that governs the alignment of spins at the points where the crystals meet. An interesting outcome of this interaction is the development of unique spin patterns at these intersection points, exhibiting the characteristics of spins flipping in opposite directions around the crystal perimeter, which could be crucial for creating advanced spin-based computing systems. Additionally, the research discovered another unique spin configuration arising from this interaction, where the spins point perpendicular to the crystal planes and reverse polarity between adjacent crystals, exhibiting rotational asymmetry under mirror reflection. The presence of this spin configuration can give rise to the movement of localized spins when the crystals are oriented at an angle to each other, again emphasizing the potential for unusual spin-based computing properties. These insights provide a framework for understanding the complex spin interactions in materials with chiral crystals, opening up the possibility of exploring similar phenomena in other 2D ferromagnetic materials.

Through numerical simulations, we investigate the impact of angular velocity profiles on dynamo mechanisms similar to those of the Sun. The study reveals that the type of rotation profile influences both the type of dynamo and the stars' magnetic cycles. Self-sustained magnetic cycles are possible in slower-rotating stars due to an optimal balance between the effects of shear and omega-effect, and it's found that this occurs at lower rotation rates than previously thought, within a relatively narrow range of rotational periods. The outcome of the study suggests that a similar mechanism to Alzheimer's disease may exist in solar-type stars, and that their magnetic cycles could be triggered in slowly-rotating stars through external forces, such as tidal interactions or tidal waves, which engage the star's internal dynamics.

Deep frameworks that process multiple types of unstructured data have shown great potential for accurate classification, but effective extraction of features from multiple sources remains a major challenge, especially when precise labels are scarce. The application of a single modality transfer learning often fails when combining more than one modality due to the complex relationship between their respective data. Self-supervised learning has emerged as a key solution by utilizing unsupervised or weakly labeled data to enhance multiple modalities. In this research, a new deep framework named Universal K-fan Multimodal Deep Framework with Shared Representations (UKMSR) is proposed to effectively handle multiple modalities with limited labels through self-supervised learning. The UKMSR framework employs separate autoencoders for each modality to generate self-supervised features independently before combining and aggregating them into a unified feature set. The proposed framework was experimentally validated on three datasets consisting of images, texts, and combined image-text pairs, namely EMNLT, STL10, and CIFAR100, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving superior classification performance over state-of-the-art methods while efficiently transferring knowledge across different modalities to improve performance with limited labeled data.

The unpredicted behaviors arising from inconsistent thread executions pose significant
issues, causing both functional failures and security vulnerabilities in real-world systems.
Current validation tools often fail to detect thread bugs, primarily due to limitations
imposed during analysis. In this research, we introduce McMini, an enhanced and adaptable
model checker focused on detecting thread defects. Building upon the foundation of
Fine-Grained Partial-Order Reduction (DPOR), McMini efficiently generates a limited set
of representative thread executions for a given program. Model checking with McMini
demonstrates a high detection rate for both existing and established thread bugs in
test suites and successfully identifies a new variant of a commonly observed error known as the
ABBA error. To enhance its performance analysis capabilities and real-world applicability,
we developed several configurable features and two optimization strategies for specific scenarios.
These features and optimizations allow users to customize McMini's evaluation process
according to their requirements. As a result, McMini achieves a balanced and efficient
trade-off between various constraints, ensuring that it can effectively and
successfully run in real-world scenarios.

In an effort to stop the spread of false information, governments have proposed limiting users' abilities to share messages on WhatsApp. The plan is to require users to log in and identify themselves, allowing the government to monitor suspicious activity. However, this idea may backfire, as it could actually accelerate the dissemination of misinformation. Our goal is to investigate the feasibility of this idea, using both fieldwork and a simulation model to understand the dynamics of information propagation within our team.

We analyze a population model featuring a multitype branching structure with potentially infinite many alleles, and derive precise limits for frequency-based proportions within this framework. This research builds on and extends the findings of a prior study specific to finite population sizes, while also drawing connections to infinite population models and highlighting the role of tail behavior in finite models.

This paper explores the concept of incorporating a specialized counteraction mechanism into spoofing detection systems. We propose integrating a novel activation function called "Vigilant" within the feature extraction portion of the system. This activation function operates on the principle of filtering out unfamiliar samples, effectively preventing unknown voices from bypassing the system. Our approach complements existing spoofing detection methods by adding a layer of protection at a different point in the system architecture. Extensive experiments have been conducted to validate the proposed method's efficacy.

We've developed a new class of supersymmetric inflation models with superior
properties. In standard Local Supersymmetry models, the gravitational sector
consists of three complex fields - heavy for two and one field suitable for
driving inflation. To simplify, we proposed earlier a method involving the
separation of the two heavy fields using a locally supersymmetric version of
the Goldstone equivalence theorem. This effectively reduces the gravitational
sector's complexity without adding extra assumptions. Furthermore, we now
apply the same logic to isolate the scalar component within the remaining
gravitational field, leaving us with a locally supersymmetric model consisting
of a specific 'light' field within the gravitational sector, along with a
predictably monomial form for the inflaton's potential. These new models are
not only mathematically elegant but also make precise predictions for
cosmological parameters with enhancements to reheating and decay rates.

Research on spatial asymmetry in photon pairs generated through parametric down-conversion has been expanded by employing two-dimensional detection systems and associated algorithms. We demonstrate a correlation pattern that is more pronounced in the horizontal direction compared to the vertical. This outcome is attributed to variations in the birefringence properties of the crystal along its length. Our findings are supported by both experimental evidence and computational algorithms.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as a leading platform for quantum computing, but current readout methods are limited by the spatial scale they can probe, limiting their ability to characterize defect qubits in redundant architectures. To overcome this constraint, a new readout system was developed that utilizes terahertz spectroscopy and near-field scanning to resolve nanometer-scale fields within the circuit. This technique enables simultaneous global readout and local probing of the circuit, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of its quantum properties. To demonstrate its efficacy, the system was applied to a transmon qubit incorporated into two different architectures: a simple loop and a larger loop containing a Josephson junction loop junction. By comparing the two, the authors demonstrate the capability of the technique to investigate the qubit in a more complex architecture, thereby paving the way for its use in studying qubits with loop-holes.

We investigate how the cardinality of a set $X$ is related to its ability to partition the real line into subsets of type A or B. Let $\mathfrak{b}$ and $\mathfrak{d}$ denote最小 values for which the set of A is unbounded and uncountable, respectively. It was demonstrated by Brendle that $|\mathfrak{b}|+\aleph_0 \le \mathfrak{c}$ holds true if there exists a partition of the reals into $\mathfrak{b}$ A-set and B-set. In this paper, we expand on this demonstration by proving that $\aleph_1 \le \mathfrak{b} + \mathfrak{d} + 1$ holds as a consequence, provided that the reals are partitioned into $\mathfrak{b}$ A-set and $\mathfrak{d}$ B-set. Furthermore, we examine specific instances of these partitions, focusing on those with particular properties of their sections, and establish new inequalities by showing that $\aleph_1 \le \mathfrak{b} + \mathfrak{d} + 1$ holds true under these conditions. We demonstrate the accuracy of these inequalities by presenting instances where the equalities occur in the Laver model. These demonstrations build upon previous research by Baumgartner, Cossey, and Kunen. We also establish new results by proving that $\aleph

In a simulated market environment, we analyze if introducing new strategies forces existing ones to cede some of their advantages due to market limitations. Various methods are for different assets and rely on model predictions, including both numerical models and those without any predictive component. Our results show techniques without a predictive element are particularly susceptible to financial downturns in the "black swan" event.

Since its creation in the 1970s, network protocol analysis has seen significant advancement but remains a difficult problem. Self-optimizing network applications, which adapt transmission settings like packet dimensions, introduce dynamism that complicates automatic identification. This study evaluates the effectiveness of a source-based network monitoring system in a dynamic environment. Specifically, we assess how packet headers, such as length and sequence, influence the performance of a well-known open-source tool. Our analysis reveals that incorporating dynamic high-length packet headers improves the tool's protocol identification accuracy.

We investigate the dynamic connection between superconducting and normal sections in a system containing both magnons and photons, where superconducting layers are placed in close proximity to magnetic materials. Through analytical and numerical methods, it's demonstrated that superconducting materials act as effective barriers, preventing the transmission of thermal energy between the magnon cloud and surrounding normal materials. Additionally, it's found that increased coupling strength of the superconductor leads to decreased thermal conductivity and a longer relaxation time of the magnons.

This research introduces ZDL, a groundbreaking distributed learning framework designed for efficient machine learning operations on large datasets, which is an essential component of AI systems. Unlike existing distributed learning methods that focus on network size reduction, ZDL is specifically developed for datasets, significantly lowering communication requirements and data transfer costs. To address data heterogeneity issues in distributed learning, a new technique called Local Label Learning (LLL) is integrated into ZDL. LLL enables each device to perform a local learning task and share predictions with others to create a novel, shared label through consensus-based label space alignment. The effectiveness of the ZDL framework is demonstrated on two distinct datasets, including a comprehensive, publicly available 87-class bird species collection and a proprietary 25,000-image dataset, both comprising audio categories. Notably, using ZDL with the audio datasets reveals its ability to achieve high accuracy on novel classes with a minimum number of communication rounds and significantly reduced bandwidth requirements compared to central learning methods.

There is a growing interest in the applications of Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states in the fields of information processing and information theory. Since many of these states are designed for specific purposes, there is a need for reliable verification that they are suitable for these applications. Consequently, there is a significant demand for a versatile assessment method that can handle various GHZ states in any specific area. Traditional methods, such as the Mermin inequality, mesoscopic projections, and minimal measurements, are limited to GHZ states in particular dimensions. However, they become computationally infeasible as the dimension increases. To address this challenge, we introduce a comprehensive GHZ state assessment method in any dimension. This involves the selection of a code based on the Hamming matrix, which allows for the identification of maximal and multi-point correlations. Furthermore, we present the mesoscopic assessment protocol that relies on the Hamming matrix, for which a suitable family is chosen to efficiently verify GHZ states in any dimension. Our protocol reduces the required number of mesoscopic assessments to O(nlogn) in terms of n. Finally, we demonstrate an experimental setup using a 12-qubit system that successfully obtains the relevant GHZ states, and our classical simulation confirms that this assessment method is practically feasible even with current technology.

This study presents a low-overhead communication system known as MultiInput SingleOutput (Multiuser MISO) with adjustable Meta-Electromagnetic Surfaces (IRS). Following a high-dimensional main path signal transmission, the signal is reflected by the adjustable IRS to additional low-dimension paths, making it impractical to characterize all the high-dimensional and varying backscatter paths due to their different characteristics. Therefore, this study proposes a method called cascaded channel estimation (CCE) that reduces complexity and allows the optimization of IRS for direct and backscatter paths simultaneously. CCE exploits the shared signal transmission assumption and treats the direct and backscatter phases as a single joint MultiDimensional MultiInput SingleOutput (MultiDimensional MISO) channel. Mathematical formulations are also introduced to achieve optimal IRS for both direct and backscatter signals. Simulation results confirm that CCE outperforms traditional methods and that the proposed CCE with optimal IRS setting surpasses the best performance achievable through optimal IRS CCE.

Analysis of regional news coverage of the COVID-19 pandemic by U.S. publishers reveals significant disparities and nuances. While major national outlets faced consistent challenges, their top stories and editorial content approaches varied widely from one region to another. We examined content frequencies, narrative styles, and production methods across 16 selected regions over an 11-month period. We also evaluated the impact of local news consistency on public health data, comparing changes in story volume and death rates. Finally, we investigated potential correlations between news types, header content, and audience engagement metrics like reader counts and ad revenue.

The fundamental skill of counting is a crucial aspect of cognitive development that supports a child's cognitive growth. Recent research has utilized neural networks to analyze the acquisition of counting skills, but these models have been limited to understanding instantaneous relationships and unable to capture the skill acquisition process. In response, this study presents an iterative model based on recurrent neural networks, incorporating social influences, to effectively model the progression of counting skill acquisition. Furthermore, the proposed model's results indicate that its outputs align with empirical data, and it demonstrates that children's skill acquisition abilities are enhanced by their social interactions, as well as their existing knowledge.

A variation of the Bloom filter called a xor filter offers an even smaller and lighter approximation by employing xoring instead of logical operations for element addition. Despite its smaller size, the OR operations used in Bloom filters can lead to quicker growth and lower false positive rates over time. In contrast, xor filters grow solely based on element count, resulting in lower size and quicker query times due to single bitwise operations. A new algorithm has been developed to mitigate the issues of dynamic xor filters, enabling double the capacity with a 50% reduction in size. Further optimization has shown that using larger bitflips over smaller n-values can reduce the filter's size even more, for example using m/n = 125/20 results in a 20% decrease in size compared to m/n = 255/2. Quicker analysis has also demonstrated xor filters are 10-20 times faster than Bloom filters and CNF structures while being 1000 times swifter than CNF structures in hardware settings.

In this investigation, correlations between topological properties of convex sets in a plane and geometric properties of non-archimedean fields are explored. We explore how properties of the convex topology on a plane relate to the geometry of a valuation ring's associated boundary surface. These relationships illuminate connections between topological convexity and complex geometric valuation theory. A particular focus is placed on the equivalence between topological convexity and the non-archimedean nature of a valuation, which yields novel insights into the understanding of convex geometry through a lens of algebraic geometry.

To assess the impact of market trends on investment outcomes, we suggest a new dataset that incorporates market trends for common stock markets, based on the sequence of past market transactions. This new dataset, which we refer to as Market Trend Data (MTD), is comprised of four key elements: execution price trends, quantity trends, cost of execution, and trade volume. The MTD effect on investment returns is quantified through the use of a modified version of the industry standard industry average and in-house pricing models. By analyzing the MTD, we find significant evidence of a notable phenomenon known as "market trend persistence," which implies that the market trend at the time of trading can have a significant impact on the investment outcome.

The training of artificial intelligence models utilizing federated learning maintains user privacy, as data remains on a central server. However, despite benefits, a major challenge with federal learning is model robustness, as malicious users can compromise the integrity of trained models. This paper addresses two primary concerns - enhancing model robustness and protecting individual user data - through the development of FLVoogd, a novel federated learning framework. The introduced mechanism incorporates statistical tests and weighted averaging algorithms, which efficiently tackle several issues often overlooked in federated learning research. The efficacy of FLVoogd is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments, including simulations with malicious users and advanced attack methods on diverse datasets and models. The data for these experiments is publicly available, allowing for the replication of our findings.

This study establishes a link between the feasibility of sim-to-real transfer in neural network-based navigation and the employability of feature matching in visual tasks. The theoretical framework is supported by empirical evidence, drawn from both synthetic and real images of objects. The research relies on an assumption that the degree of order in a system can be measured by the entropy of its microstates. The results indicate that employing picture gradients as a metric to assess image 'order' allows for the creation of a reusable protocol to evaluate sim-to-real transferability. The proposed approach is straightforward, task-independent, and potentially facilitates the development of more robust neural policies for visual navigation.

Significant progress has been made in the field of deepfake creation, with several state-of-the-art methods emerging. However, current advancements are primarily based on the concept of using a one-to-one mapping between facial images and videos. This relies on precise person alignment, which poses significant obstacles when applied to unconstrained media such as photographs or clips featuring multiple individuals. To overcome these limitations, our research delves into adapting deepfake creation techniques to handle one-to-many mappings and presents two innovative approaches: Adaptive Face Synthesis and Video Object Detection Masking. Furthermore, while deepfake detection methods have also seen advancements, they are largely ineffective when confronted with unconstrained legitimate data. To tackle this challenge, we propose a conceptually simple yet highly effective technique called Gradient Re-weighting. Through extensive testing on a comprehensive dataset known as Forensicnet, we demonstrate the superiority of our solutions on both creation and detection fronts.

The existence of vast liquid oceans on sub-Neptune exoplanets has been hypothesized, yet verifying their presence through observational methods remains challenging. Previous research proposed that the presence of dissolved water within an exoplanet's atmosphere could serve as an indicator of past or present oceans. However, the validity of this method was disputed due to the possibility that the same chemical balances could result from gas-phase reactions rather than indicating the existence of oceans. We present an alternative approach that utilizes a different chemical reaction system to distinguish between concealed and hidden oceans, relying on a solubility balance that is solely dependent on the depth of a convection zone. Our model, which assumes the presence of an ancient ocean, demonstrates that a particular ratio of methane to hydrogen in the atmosphere of a temperate exoplanet could indicate the existence of a concealed ocean. In a randomized survey of exoplanets, a significant majority that display secondary molecular features also meet the criteria for indicating an ancient ocean, suggesting that a future telescope, such as the 30m Exoplanet Research Facility, could potentially verify the existence of these concealed oceans.

Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to learn basic tasks in language and audio processing, however they are limited in explaining how the human brain overcomes these tasks. This study investigates the sequence learning abilities of RNNs by focusing on the effects of neural signaling characteristics. Utilizing the popular IMGSAT dataset, researchers found that a vanilla RNN model was unable to learn the full range of tasks as effectively as other architectures, due in part to the complex relationship between its neurons. By modifying the neural network's activation and spike thresholds to mimic biological processes, they were able to significantly improve its performance. Furthermore, they found that a specific type of spiking rule (the threshold rule) allowed the network to learn sequences faster than other options. These results suggest that simply adjusting the neural network's biological properties can lead to significant improvements in sequence learning ability.

This report documents the findings from the 2021 October Out-of-Context Challenge.
The purpose of this document is to confirm the winning entries identified in the challenge's final announcement.
The report starts by outlining the rules and constraints of the competition.
Subsequently, it presents the criteria used to evaluate performance in the competition.
The report then highlights the key aspects of the submitted solutions.
Finally, it addresses the technical difficulties encountered during the competition.

This study introduces a novel algorithm that utilizes the reduced basis method in conjunction with generalized polynomial chaos expansions to address complex computational uncertainty analysis problems. The algorithm starts with a random variable of unknown functionality f, which the generalized polynomial chaos expansion approximates as f~ = Σ a_k k(x), where the coefficients a_k = a_k are to be determined. The generalized polynomial chaos expansion is then verified using the eigenvalue problem's solution space. The general framework has been applied to two specific cases, involving solving a stochastic boundary value problem and a matrix inverse a~ = a^-1_B, which have been demonstrated using a finite element discretization-based solver and the least squares minimization approach, respectively.

We have developed an innovative adaptive algorithm that detects and isolates changes in a discrete-time system that evolves over time. The algorithm works with data that is observed at regular intervals but may only be partially see the system's internal state. It assumes that the system's changes occur within a limited set of possible variations. We have formulated mathematical equations based on the distance between different variations and derived a method to calculate the likelihood of each change. We have derived lower and upper limits for these likelihood calculations. We propose an algorithm that uses these limits to identify the exact moment a change occurs and determine which variation it corresponds to. We have demonstrated through theoretical analysis and practical tests that our algorithm successfully detects and isolates changes with a minimum level of error.

The analysis of light from distant galaxies enables astronomers to trace the pace of star formation over vast periods, revealing valuable information about the universe's evolution over time. To achieve this, spectroscopy is employed to break down light into its component colors, allowing for precise measurements of both the speed and evolution of star formation processes. The following discussion highlights the progress made in analyzing the speed and evolution of star formation through spectroscopy, particularly in exploring distant, small galaxies, and outlines the upcoming advancements that will arise from the Speed and Evolution of Populations (SeEp) program using the Speed, Evolution, and Abundance (SeA) methodology utilizing the Powerful Optical Spectroscopic Telescope, or POST, telescope.

Given a continuous action of a profinite group $G$ on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, we can define a action spectrum, which is a function from the dual space of irreducible complex characters of $G$ to the integers. This action spectrum satisfies key properties: it's $G$-invariant under conjugation, stable under Gelfand-Tsetlin transformations, and respects equivalent actions. Additionally, there's a formula involving the action spectrum and the fixed point set of the action. Unlike previous work, our action spectrum can take negative values.

A common challenge in developing NLP models for document processing is efficiently extracting valuable information from visually intricate documents, such as invoices, due to a lack of available labeled training data. To overcome this limitation, we propose two techniques to decrease labeling costs, which we test on a real-world invoice dataset. By applying these methods, our extraction performance is nearly as good as using fully-supervised training on an entire set of annotated invoices. One technique involves creating a mini-set of labeled invoices through random sampling to train both a document classification model and a generic transformer-based extractor, which then gets applied to the remaining data. We find that this approach yields results close to supervised training on the full dataset, and also reveals the value of class balance for accurate document classification. We also present a technique that combines the outputs of multiple trained models to identify and mark the relevant sections on unlabeled documents, which then get human-reviewed, leading to a significant 70% reduction in labeling expenses while maintaining near-superior performance.

The magnetic transition in EuS near its critical temperature results in a dramatic shift from a metal to a insulator. Researchers have found that thin EuS layers on InAs can retain their metallicity below the bulk's magnetic transition temperature. A study using a detailed model to represent the electronic structure of the EuS/InAs interface has revealed that the subgap states in the spectroscopic data can be attributed to specific magnetic states and a covalent bond between the Eu and S atoms and the InAs material. Additionally, the bonding arrangement at the interface influences the charge transfer between the EuS and InAs, which could lead to the insulator characteristics observed in the EuS/InAs data.

A significant result by Wadge demonstrated that continuous functions can partition Borel sets into equivalence classes under the relation of reducibility. It has since been established that each Borel equivalence class contains a representative that is either regular or has a regular hyperspace. This paper presents two contributions: first, an efficient characterization of Borel classes using the concept of boundary width, and its application in determining the topological category of a set via its boundary width; second, a novel method for constructing boundary representations of non-analytic sets, which yields examples of Borel sets whose boundaries are analytic but are not $\sigma$-compact.

Deep neural networks (DNNs), being highly parameterized, often pose computational and memory constraints on embedded systems. This challenge has driven the surge in research on DNN model compression, which not only boosts inference speed but also enhances the feasibility of training via model pruning. Current DNN model compression research primarily focuses on improving model size and inference latency but neglects the effect on training time. Our investigation into post-pruning and model rejuvenation reveals that ClickTrain can achieve substantial improvements, reducing both model size and accuracy loss while also decreasing the number of training steps by a factor of up to 7.5, thus establishing a framework for end-to-end efficient and precise DNN optimization.

This study integrates modal operators into the DLK system, a logical framework that governs natural language inference, by adding new rules to its axioms. The research demonstrates how these modal operators interact within the system and under what conditions they behave in a specific way. Furthermore, the study validates a fundamental mathematical principle - the distribution of these modal operators is both a logical consequence of their definition and a sufficient condition for their implementation, as shown through a sound and complete system.

The observation of gravitational waves (GWs) from binary neutron star (NS-NS) mergers has been limited so far, but expectations for observing binary black hole - neutron star (BH-NS) and binary neutron star mergers are higher. Advances in detecting GWs are anticipated due to the substantial improvements in the sensitivity of the detector, the accumulation of empirical data, and development of theoretical models. However, the detection and distinction of binary inspiral signals from background noise become increasingly more difficult given varying detector sensitivity and diverse populations of compact objects involved. Recent advancements in machine learning have the potential to resolve this issue by providing an efficient and adaptable approach to classifying these signals. In this context, we will explore the application of a sophisticated neural network, the LeCun-Cortesson architecture, to identify and categorize GW signals based on the time-frequency patterns they exhibit.

Our analysis of photometric data from TESS for the planet-hosting star TOI-5542 utilizes a versatile transit-fit model that effectively accounts for limb darkening and blur induced by the blur effect. By incorporating TESS and WASP photometric findings along with radial velocity measurements from the SPHERE spectroscopy on the HIRES instrument at the Keck telescope, we obtained a newly determined set of parameters including a determined orbital period of 628.65 days with an estimated measurement error of 6.12 days. This period led to the discovery of the radius of the planet, which was calculated as 1.10 times the radius of Jupiter with an estimated error of 0.05, and the mass of the planet, which was found to be 1.41 times the mass of Jupiter with an estimated error of 0.15. Additionally, we calculated the semi-major axis as 1.23 AU with an estimated error of 0.05 AU. This discovery aligns with the observed trend of large-radius exoplanets having longer orbital periods as reported by Fressin et al. Moreover, the observed trend of the relationship between stellar metallicity and planetary metallicity is consistent with the findings of Gao et al. Finally, we determined the equilibrium temperature of the planet to be 199.78 Kelvin with an estimated error of 0.5 kelvin.

This paper explores how to optimize a Markov choice problem by selecting an optimal policy from a set of feasible policies, with the goal of maximizing the expected reward. A new method using gradient projection is proposed to resolve the practical difficulties of projection in this area. The method relies on converting the original problem into a constrained linear program and demonstrating its feasibility and optimality using gradient and dual variables, respectively. The relationship between the constrained and unconstrained versions of the problem is explored, which is subsequently used to develop a novel method for solving the constrained problem by leveraging the optimal solution of the unconstrained problem. The performance of this method is verified using numerical experiments on benchmark Markov decision problems and a real-world cancer treatment selection task, with results showing that it has a low computational cost and provides interpretable projection.

This paper presents an innovative approach to offline handwritten mathematical notation recognition, leveraging deep learning. This method utilizes two neural networks, a CNN for extracting feature maps and a FNN for generating corresponding labels, with the framework's efficacy demonstrated on the ISTH-4 and offline LATEX datasets. Notably, the best results on the ISTH-4 dataset exhibited an accuracy of 98.8%, while the most impressive outcome on the offline LATEX dataset achieved an accuracy of 97.9%.

A new approach to computing the cohomology of complex manifolds involves representing cohomology classes as sections of specific sheaves constructed from polynomial functions. These sheaves are formed using a superpotential and its auxiliary functions, along with supercharges that increase cohomology degree. In this framework, one can define an infinite-dimensional supersymmetric quantum mechanics. The central question is whether this quantum mechanics exhibits a "non-trivial" cohomology. In cohomology, there's an infinite complex with a nilpotent supercharge, and the key question is whether the cohomology is "trivial" (all sections are exact) or "non-trivial" (there are exact nilpotent sections). The challenge lies in determining the structure of non-trivial cohomology. This paper presents an infinite-dimensional SQM model and computes its non-trivial cohomology, demonstrating an infinite-dimensional analog of sheaf cohomology. The model features a superpotential with a specific polynomial form, and the cohomology is shown to be isomorphic to specific vector spaces. The vector spaces in question are specific hypercohomology groups of a complex manifold, and the result can be interpreted as a dimensional version of sheaf cohomology. The result can also be seen as an infinite-dimensional analog of sheaf cohomology, and the result can be seen as a hypercohomology group of a complex manifold.

The random nature of events in dynamic network processes is closely linked to the variability of inter-event occurrences. This connection has significant implications for network design and its impact on process performance. To gain a comprehensive understanding, we employ both analytical and simulation approaches to examine the random variability of the interaction process within a network of any complex structure. The results show that random variability consistently increases with the network's complexity. Additionally, we reveal that the standard measure of variability for inter-event times does not adequately represent the variability of occurrence times. Instead, we propose and validate a new metric for assessing variability at any given time step. This metric can provide a complete assessment of variability across any network structure. Our analysis also demonstrates that the variability of node and network processes can be accurately predicted using only the topology of the network and the probability distribution of individual inter-event times. This capability allows for detailed analysis of variability in any network using a post-processing approach. This is achieved by conducting an in-depth study of node and network behavior during a single, hypothetical "randomization" of the network process. This approach can be applied to all networks that are driven by sporadic events.

Our enhanced Actor-Critic (EAC) reinforcement learning algorithm improves policy exploration and academic literacy in action selection. Traditional Actor-Critic methods struggle to effectively explore the state-action space due to their reliance on greedy policies. We address this limitation by incorporating the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) method, a widely-used technique in robust Markov Decision Process exploration. The HMC method leverages physical systems' conservation laws to construct a structured exploration mechanism, ensuring stable policy-learning. Simulations demonstrate that EAC accelerates convergence, produces more consistent policies, and generates more diverse exploratory actions.

A straightforward, computer-verifyable proof is offered for the statement that any prime number less than or equal to 41 is followed by a prime at a minimal gap of 2, within a number up to 2620.  Consequently, the Twin Prime Hypothesis can be formally demonstrated as long as the specific exception of 37 and 41 is confirmed.  Furthermore, the broader statement of the hypothesis can also be visually demonstrated on a separate page.

A primary goal in improving the performance of Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) is enhancing their localization capabilities, which involves determining their precise position. The effectiveness of Positioning, Navigation and Timing (PNT) systems relies on high-precision sonar positing technology, however its application is hindered by various factors including varying scales, noise levels, and differences in coordinate systems. Resolving these disparities before processing data for position calculation is a time-consuming process that limits real-time usability. Our research introduces an innovative immediate sonar blending approach for immediate integration within a layered navigation framework, allowing real-time position estimation without pre-processing data to resolve disparities in scale, noise levels, and coordinate systems.

Nereid, a small moon of Neptune, shares similar composition and albedo characteristics with many other trans-Neptunian objects. We studied the spectral properties of Nereid using the NIRC2 instrument on the Keck II telescope, and found a low-albedo surface with no distinct spectral features beyond a general red slope. Our analysis revealed that Nereid has a low-iron meteorite-like composition, and its spectral characteristics can be explained by a mixture of water ice and tholins, rather than a pure water-ice surface. We found that Nereid's water-ice content is around 80-90%, and its phase angle albedo ranges from 0.076 to 0.093, and its thermal-emissivity is estimated to be 0.000076 ± 0.0000076 K^-1.

Studies on lower triangular matrix rings have been conducted individually. This work examines surfaces defined over these rings, applying established methods from affine and projective geometry. Building on existing findings, we analyze these surfaces, consider their point counts, and examine related geometry. Furthermore, we introduce a new method to define and investigate linked affine and projective spaces and surfaces.

A specific type of sequence, known as a Tukey-sequence with models, is employed to demonstrate the validity of two P-w-theorems developed by Pawlikowski. First, a notion of a model-free partial order with P-w properties is defined. Subsequently, it is proven that two such orders satisfy the intersection theorem when combined. Furthermore, it is shown that two specific types of orders satisfy the crossing theorem with respect to models from different cardinalities.

Building on Fessler, Hartl, and Kamien's Bayesian approach to pessimism in dynamic treatment strategies, we explore its implications under uncertain environments. Their research found that pessimism leads to early adoption under concave uncertainty, delayed adoption under linear expectations, and early adoption when combining both. Contrarily, our results show that when pessimism evolves over time, it has no consistent effect on the timing of new technology implementation. Specifically, we find that early adoption under linear expectations is possible due to the influence of Bayesian learning, which causes agents to gradually shift towards optimal action levels. Moreover, Bayesian pessimism causes a unique non-stationary threshold that evolves over time, unaffected by the degree of pessimism.

Dualities play a significant role in the development of efficient recognition techniques and transformations within the realms of decodings and compressions. This study explores duals specifically within the context of the singular homology theory, utilizing Z_m as the coefficient group. It recognizes that the dual in this context isn't strictly speaking homeopathic in nature. Furthermore, the investigation establishes connections between various invariants through formulae. Subsequently, specific applications related to the detection of holes and computing entropy are demonstrated.

We've developed an efficient way to calculate the cluster update in the complex $E_8$ lattice model, allowing for precise simulations of an all-qubit system. The complexification of this lattice was initially proposed by Ohgaki et al. as a method to study the highly entangled ground state without relying on a matrix product state. Our procedure involves calculating the complex probability amplitudes and verifying the occurrence of quantum entanglement. Additionally, we've confirmed the existence of quantum contextuality. However, our analysis also shows that the cluster state's entanglement is not as strong as expected, while we found contextuality to persist at lower temperatures.

Our research shows that the Kohn Luttinger scenario can lead to multiple-body Cooper pairing, which may serve as a prerequisite for various exotic states and a potential underlying mechanism for some observed experiments involving twisted systems. Within the research, we found that by considering the two-dimensional flat-band system with the $C_2$ symmetry, we discovered multiple-body Cooper pairing between corner modes due to the divergence of the effective mass near this mode, which increases by its order rather than its square mass. Additionally, we found that a similar mechanism can cause an unusual pairing between the mode of a two-dimensional winding and its counterpart with a reversed winding, resulting in a precursor to the vortex state. Lastly, we found that in systems with hexagonal symmetry, there is an anomalous pairing between the mode of a Weyl node and its node with the opposite chirality, which may lead to an underlying mechanism for the recent observation of zero-energy modes at vortices.

We consider and partially resolve a problem regarding linked groups in the context of set theory without the Axiom of Choice. Specifically, we have established theorems that demonstrate, for certain types of groups, they are linked if and only if certain conditions are met. These results generalize earlier work on countable groups and expand the understanding of linked groups without relying on the Axiom of Choice. In addition, we have shown a specific exception to a previously thought to be universally valid criterion for when two groups are linked.

Presence-absence data has become increasingly significant across various fields, including ecology and biology, reflecting the availability or occurrence of entities like species or genes. The analysis of such data typically involves dimensionality reduction through the identification of latent associations between entities. Given the distinct characteristics of this data type, conventional clustering methods may not effectively apply, necessitating a thorough evaluation of various techniques. In this study, a comprehensive framework for assessing clustering algorithms is developed, focusing on specific features typical of high-dimensional presence-absence data. The framework involves simulating a large dataset, for which extensive results from real-world studies serve as reliable benchmarks. Upon analyzing nearly 30 clustering algorithms, random forest-based and kernel-based methods emerged as the most effective, outperforming traditional algorithms, especially in cases with sparse data. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that method selection is crucial when processing this type of data, and recommendations are provided for evaluating clustering performance.

In recent years, salient object detection has become a major focus in computer vision research, leading to the development of numerous advanced methods that rely on the integration of RGB and RGB-D technologies. This paper presents a unified approach for salient object detection that leverages RGB and RGB-D data to improve accuracy and adaptability. The method employs a novel multi-scale feature extraction technique that combines the advantages of both technologies to achieve high precision in salient region identification. Specifically, the proposed method exploits the inherent characteristics of RGB and RGB-D data to generate a multi-scale framework that enhances the robustness and efficiency of salient object detection. Furthermore, this unified framework enhances the method's compatibility and performance translation across different datasets. The method's performance was evaluated on several standard datasets, demonstrating superior results compared to existing methods. Notably, the proposed method achieved exceptional results on the SOD, DUT, SDO, HDS, HRS, WED, DAVIS, MOTS, CO-SOT, DISSOT, Real-time Multi-Object Tracking, and SOT-20 datasets, outperforming multiple state-of-the-art methods on each dataset. The source code for the proposed method is available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/FeiFei-Fei/salient-object-detector.

The UM-IU@LING system participated in the SemEval-2019 work on identifying aggression in social media content by determining whether a given tweet was single-entity, double-entity, or not aggressive. The challenge also required flagging tweets containing hate speech. A combination of different machine learning techniques was utilized at UM-IU@LING, which involved using BERT and SVM models.

This paper explores the fractional parts that result from dividing symmetrical numbers by non-zero integers. It establishes the proof for a conjecture previously proposed by Gonzalez-Davidson and provides related findings for various types of number patterns. The study employs a unified framework using a polygonal number system and a generalised hexagonal figure. By doing so, it delves into the properties of symmetrical and antisymmetrical numbers, presenting both theoretical and practical evidence to support a hypothesis put forth by Gonzalez-Davidson.

Computed Tomography (CT) is widely utilized in various sectors, including medical diagnostics and industrial inspections. In order to enhance its effectiveness, a novel CT reconstruction technique has been developed. This innovative technique combines the advantages of continuous and discrete reconstruction methods. It starts with a continuous model that incorporates the Materials Decomposition (MD) into the imaging process itself. A unique transformation is then applied, converting the intractable problem into a simpler one. This technique is supported by the Moreau-Rosenbrock Theorem, and it uses the transformation known as the Endmembers Table. A reconstruction problem is formulated using the transformed problem as its foundation, and it incorporates various constraints, including physical limitations, to guarantee the coherence, non-negativity, and sparsity of the solution. This constraint-laden optimization problem is solved efficiently using the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers, which it simplifies into two manageable sub-problems. These sub-problems can be solved using closed-form and the Alternating Directions Methods of Multipliers methods. The proposed algorithm demonstrates remarkable convergence and stability. It succeeds, especially when low X-ray energy ranges are used, and it outperforms current state-of-the-art reconstruction techniques. It also excels when dealing with high sensor noise levels.

Recent advancements in handwritten text recognition have largely relied on vast,
uniform datasets. However, creating such datasets is both labor-intensive and impractical, particularly for regions with diverse writing styles and limited sample availability. To address this challenge, this research proposes a method for generating balanced training data from regional handwriting samples without requiring additional input other than a few examples of standard text samples. The approach generates synthetic training data by creating artificial handwriting samples based on the characteristics of the provided samples and ensures a diverse distribution of the training data through weighted sampling. Comprehensive evaluations on a comprehensive evaluation benchmark reveal that the proposed method surpasses handwriting-style transfer techniques and rivals the performance of models trained on extensive, balanced datasets of single-shot handwriting classification and recognition tasks.

Utilizing ab initio methods to study nuclear properties, specifically through the IM-SGF approach's application to very heavy nuclei, has been made possible through advancements in supercomputing capabilities. This study evaluates the feasibility of this ab initio method by analyzing the properties of the 110Cd nucleus. For this purpose, multiple sets of 2-Nucleon interactions, generated from distinct EFT-Efficient Nucleon Multiplet representations, are considered. The results are further refined by applying various 3-Nucleon interactions. By comparing the calculations to experimental data, the study demonstrates that existing IM-SGF code can effectively utilize the EM interaction, EM 3N, and EH 3N operators to produce reasonable agreements in binding energies for nuclei as heavy as 208Pb. This study also highlights the implications of varying EM, 3N, and RHo interactions when employing EM, EM 3N, and EH 3N operators.

Quantum systems exhibiting topological characteristics are renowned for their unique properties and the edge states they possess. To shed light on the fundamental principles governing topological quantum phenomena, we employ the SSH model as a teaching tool. This model enables us to elucidate the topological nature of quantum systems using the Chern number and quantum charge density operator, offering a clearer understanding of the phenomenon. Furthermore, we investigate the concept of charge pumping in relation to topological features. To delve deeper into the local charge density fluctuations and the observable manifestations of topological properties, we apply time-resolved quantum spectroscopy using a coupling with light.

This study examines the compactness of composition operators between Bergman spaces associated with certain types of convex domains in complex n-dimensional space that possess an inward-pointing boundary, specifically those similar to the unit ball and Hartogs triangle. It also investigates the compactness of a composition operator involving the Bergman spaces of two specific types of domains: the weighted Bergman space of the biunit ball and the Bergman space of the biunit ball with an exponentiated weight. Furthermore, it examines the compactness of composition operators between the Bergman spaces of the biunit ball and the polydisc.
