We utilized the results of double-loop calculations in N=4 super-Yang-Mills theory to determine the two-loop value of a specific wavelength on the five-dimensional hypersphere within a de Sitter space within AdS space. This calculation aligns with an earlier prediction made through direct dual-isospin algebra methods. The success of this calculation supports the hypothesis that holographic duality can be extended to higher-dimensional spaces and suggests a potential approach for exploring this duality in more complex scenarios.

High-performance computing on GPU memory is hampered by inefficient memory access patterns of applications, which can lead to excessive global memory transactions. The dynamic allocation of pointers exacerbates this issue, often resulting in scattered memory access patterns that reduce execution efficiency. Existing solutions for addressing this problem are primarily limited to frameworks with fixed memory allocations, leaving a significant gap in handling the dynamic memory allocations typical of object-oriented programming languages like Java and Python. This paper introduces DynaSOAr, a memory allocator designed to mitigate inefficient memory access patterns of Python and Java applications on GPUs, specifically in the domain of image processing. DynaSOAr builds on the foundation of the Split Violation Ordered Access memory access control technique, which imposes strict constraints on access patterns to facilitate efficient memory access. The method involves tracking dynamical memory allocations and simulating heap data structures to identify and enforce simulated memory addresses within blocks. The effectiveness of DynaSOAr is demonstrated through benchmark analyses, which show substantial reductions in GPU transaction costs and improved execution efficiency. The method's extension to C++ and-cedc are shown to yield additional performance benefits.

The basic models with a single U(1) U(1)_X symmetry can be comprehensively categorized only five types. Conventions that annul the conventional $U(1)_Y$ symmetry are employed and calculations concerning anomaly cancellation and x-baryon or x-lepton number violations are performed. It is observed that x-baryon or x-lepton number violations occur in the primary and tertiary models but not in the secondary, quartile, and quintile models. However, all five models facilitate a diverse range of $U(1)_X$ flavor violations, thereby leading to potentially observable effects involving charged lepton decays, flavor mixing among third-generation particles, and Higgs-dihiggs scattering. This last observation implies that a specific model may necessitate the incorporation of additional particles into its theoretical framework in order to accurately account for an experimentally determined rate of Higgs-dihiggs scattering. Additionally, the connection between the models and the leptoquark-like excited states within $U(1)_X$ mediators is examined including their decay products and media within the models' theoretical frameworks. Finally, the models are subjected to an in-depth analysis in light of various experimental constraints such as $g-2$ values of the muon, searching media for dark matter, and various particle decay rates. This comprehensive examination indicates that while all five models are theoretically viable, the primary and tertiary models appear to be the most likely to be found within nature.

A straw filled with pressurized liquid is analyzed to determine the stress it experiences, taking into account the pressurized liquid's influence on the straw's mechanical properties. The pressurized liquid inside the straw increases the straw's stiffness in both the axial and transverse directions without affecting its strength. This stress calculation is crucial for understanding how pressurized liquids affect plant and insect mechanical protection, with additional implications for understanding the mechanical protections provided by other external agents like chitin, cuticle, and mycelia. The mathematical models used in this analysis can also be applied to other biological conduit systems, such as xylem, insect tracheae, and fungal hyphae.

Recent advancements in uncertainty management have led to the development of the Credal Bayesian Framework (CBF), a concept introduced only two years ago. CBFs allow for the creation of more robust representations of uncertainties by creating a C credal set composed of n M measures that satisfy specified constraints. CBFs enable the selection of the most confident decision from n M available options under specific conditions. CBFs can be generated through the optimization of n M distinct probabilistic circuits, each tailored to fulfill a separate constraint. CBFs, however, present a significant challenge due to an intricate description structure and difficult-to-interprete nature. C+ S, an algorithm recently introduced last month, overcomes these limitations by generating C+ credal sets consisting of C+ n M representational elements and an efficient query processing time linear in the circuit size. Our work introduces a new set of algorithms that transform C+ credal sets into an expanded set of optimized C+ S credals with similar characteristics. These new algorithms ensure a defined upper limit for the probability of rejecting the optimal action by the strongest guarantee. We also introduce techniques for significantly reducing the size of the C+ credal sets while maintaining strong performance as well as offering free software for practical implementation.

We investigate the behavior of a uniform Bose-Einstein condensate accelerating under an external force. In this study, we utilize both the non-rotating frame and the rotating frame with a constant angular acceleration. In the rotating frame, we demonstrate the phenomenon of Bloch oscillations, during which we examine how the solitonic modes within the condensate interact with the accelerating force. Additionally, we utilize numerical methods to solve the Gross-Pitaevskii equation in the rotating frame, presenting two scenarios: a condensate with negligible interactions, and a condensate with strong repulsive force. Our analytical findings for the first scenario are compared with the numerical results, showing excellent agreement, while in the second scenario, the numerical approach reveals complex dynamics, including modes spinning in opposite directions that merge and generate new modes emerging from their interaction.

A code with neighbor symmetry is a type of code where all nonzero vectors have the same weight when added to any other vector. We have adapted neighbor symmetry definitions to broader quadrangle structures and proved that a code with neighbor symmetry exists if a specific dispersion property holds in one of these structures. This property suggests that a code with neighbor symmetry exists if a specific weight property holds for all lines related to any point in one of these structures. Furthermore, by applying known properties of quadrangle structures, we have established lower bounds for minimal dispersion and given examples where this bound can be achieved. These results have been verified using computational methods in all possible cases of smallest dispersion for four types of quadrangle structures.

A thorough analysis of a 2D correlation function reveals the anisotropic mass distribution within the 200pc x 100pc region of the Galactic Centre. By applying a novel method, an elliptical model was found to provide a superior fit to a substantial segment of the SMZ's mass, exceeding 90%. In contrast, traditional H-alpha emission fails to capture this anisotropic mass, while it more closely aligns with the distribution derived from massive stars and X-ray sources. These discrepancies suggest an unusual concentration of gas in the Galactic Centre. Although star formation processes were initially considered the cause, they were identified as insufficient to explain the observed effect. Consequently, the unusual gas concentration requires the involvement of additional or alternative factors.

We introduce a fundamental framework for analyzing the temporal evolution of electron and hole populations under X-ray irradiation. The model accounts for both direct ionization by an X-ray beam and indirect processes involving annealing. A generalized analytical solution is developed, and its application to the X-ray absorption edge (XAS) of materials is examined. The XAS transition probability is derived in terms of electron occupancy of inner-shell atomic orbitals. To illustrate our model, data from an experiment using synchronized hard X-ray free-electron laser and infrared laser pulses on CeO$_2$ material are analyzed, revealing the rapid excitation and slower relaxation of cerium ions.

This paper details a detector designed to map out the behavior of bandgap references, which are affected by temperature. First, we present an ultra-low voltage detector circuit that consumes a minimal amount of power while offering high accuracy, consuming only 0.6V of supply voltage and providing a gain of 49.5V/V. Next, we introduce and analyze a bandgap reference that maintains its operating voltage across a wide range of temperatures, from an initial 0.6V up to 1.8V. Through simulation using a 130nm CMOS process, we found that our detector has an impressive resolution and temperature measurement range, exhibiting a resolution of 0.24 degrees Celsius and an error margin of 1.4 degrees Celsius, and also demonstrated its ability to perform 38 million conversions per second at an average energy consumption of 1.06 nanojoules per conversion.

The generation of quantum states is typically achieved through deterministic methods, yet another approach relies on probabilistic creation followed by post-selection, commonly known as a heralded method. In this work, we explore the entanglement of quantum states, specifically focusing on the deterministic and non-degenerate methods. A quantum circuit model, known as the heralded quantum scissors, is used to create entangled states, with the help of a successful measurement outcome. Applying this principle, we have developed quantum circuits to create both pure and mixed entangled states. However, the use of the non-degenerate method presents an challenge: it is impossible to identify when entanglement occurs due to the absence of outcome indicators. We overcame this limitation by proposing a entanglement verification protocol, utilizing the Bell-channels analysis. Furthermore, the efficiency of the heralded entanglement process was improved through the combined effects of post-selection and entanglement distillation. The outcomes of this study open the door for the development of quantum technologies based on non-degenerate entanglement.

For a given parameter αααα α>1α>1α>1α>1α>1, a subset of edges in GGGEuclidean is termed an ααααα-euclidean GG spanner if the distance between any two vertices in GGGEuclidean is scaled by at most ααααα by the shortest path along the spanner's edges. We introduce the concept of virtual Euclidean spanners, a novel approach that expands upon combinatorial methods for Euclidean graph GGGEuclidean. A virtual αβαβ α>1β>1α>1β>1α>1β>1 euclidean GG spanner is defined as a subgraph consisting of edges with stretch factor ααααα and dilation factor βββββ compared to the original graph's Euclidean distance. Accurate categorization of IoT devices from remote locations is a critical task, 
yet extracting sufficient data to identify IoT device types while considering energy 
constraints is a complex issue.  This research focuses on minimizing energy 
expenditure during feature retrieval for IoT device identification.  For this 
purpose, we propose an innovative and efficient method called SCCF, which is a 
 stochastic approach based on intrinsic device responses.  Unlike traditional 
methods, SCCF selects a subset of device responses, enabling energy-saving 
extractions.  Additionally, we introduce two additional cost functions, which 
consider external energy information, and evaluate their effectiveness.  Our 
results, obtained through simulation experiments using a real IoT device dataset, 
reveal that SCCF maintains classification accuracy while significantly reducing 
energy consumption while identifying device types.

Godel modal logic T, derived from D4, its algebraic counterpart was examined in previous research. In contrast, the corresponding structures for the logic were shown to have relevant surjective mappings into classes defined by relations containing specific modal axioms. This relationship characterized determined algebras of the logic. Generalizing this concept, we explore Godel modal logics extending the basic system, considering the corresponding relational structures, where the relationship between algebraic determinacy and relational accessibility was investigated. This research was expanded upon a previously proposed relation structure for the logic, resulting in multiple, distinct relational structures being defined for the logic. Each of these structures yielded a correspondingly distinct modal logic, all of which properly extend the basic system. Furthermore, we examined the algebras corresponding to these relations, where the relationships between their respective classes were investigated.

This research explores the potential of leveraging external bilingual data to improve real-time word alignment in low-resource settings. While word alignment is a well-established task, it's particularly crucial for applications involving sign language, as it enables the association of spoken or signed words with corresponding gestures. Existing solutions often fall short in low-resource languages due to the lack of adequate training data. To address this limitation, we propose generating bilingually aligned data from multiple sources, including bilingual dictionaries, news articles, social media platforms, and other relevant sources. Our approach then utilizes this generated data to enhance the accuracy of real-time word alignment in sign language scenarios.

This research paper suggests a method for generating distorted resolvents from a monotone operator, which is applicable to both set-valued operators and convex functions. The method is then utilized in a variational game setting to establish Nash equilibria through the distorted resolvent equation. Additionally, sufficient conditions are identified under which the distorted resolvent equation can be solved by the standard resolvent operator. The convergence of an inertial iteration algorithm toward a Nash equilibrium is demonstrated in a bilevel game context. Ultimately, the proposed method is tested and evaluated through three application examples.

The theoretical framework of primordial black holes (PBHs) offers a solution to a range of challenges associated with traditional dark energy models, including the lack of a theoretical framework, the fine-tuning issue, and the coincidence problem. In this research, POPSYCLE is utilized to simulate the evolution of PBDs within a cosmological framework. We set up a simulation with a population of PBHs having a uniform mass distribution between $10^ {17}$ kg and $10^ {51}$ kg, where only those with masses less than $10^ {47}$ kg contribute to the energy density. Our findings reveal that the maximum allowable fraction of PBHs to the critical density decreases significantly over time, falling from approximately 0.04 at $z = 1$ to approximately $10^{-5}$ at present, where the fraction begins to exceed observed values. A comparative analysis with other dark models shows that the fraction falls at a slower rate model-specific rather than the nature of the dark component.

We investigate the behavior of an experimentally inspired system of geometrically modified rigid rods, reduced to a two-dimensional model where wedge-shaped rods self-assemble into sample structures. Our computational simulations using Molecular Dynamics reveal the existence of multiple free energy minima, each corresponding to a distinct stage with splay modulation, as well as the possibility of sample multistability. These findings align with previous theoretical predictions about the characteristics of entropic stability. Intermolecular forces, although weak, contribute significantly to the relative stability of different configurations. Our analysis also addresses the influence of surface roughness on the observed multistability and modulations.

Recent work on spherical Gaussian processes has been supplemented here to derive similar growth rates for static Gaussian fields on the sphere under various covariance conditions. Notably, these conditions include modulation, decay rates, and fractional differentiability. Employing recursive relations in one step, these conditions were analyzed using recursive operators based on spherical harmonics, ultimately revealing intricate connections between discrete and continuous scenarios.

We have developed a single-pixel quantum imaging method that operates undetected particle number of signal photons. It achieves this using a combination of undetected photon pairs and a statistical inference undetected based on the distribution of the remaining photon pairs. This technique implements the principle of extended coherence area. We have successfully verified our approach through both simulation and experimental verification using a undetected based on type-II BSCS source. This undetected based on type-II BSCS source has a wide range of applications in quantum imaging.

The movement of and forces within complex materials like biological and commercial products are not fully understood. We've found that the friction experienced by smooth objects moving through liquid foams is significantly lower than that observed in viscous fluids. Our finding reveals that the unique texture and structure of liquid foam walls contribute to this reduced friction. We've developed a model that explains how this reduced friction arises from the interaction between the foam and the object, with the coefficient of friction decreasing as the speed of movement and the size of the object increase. Our research has implications for understanding the behavior of materials and processes, with applications in food science and manufacturing.

This study introduces an advanced deep learning framework, specifically designed for an efficient identification of skin cancers. The proposed framework integrates three key components: (i) the identification of abnormal samples using one-dimensional convolutional neural networks and (ii) triplee loss, a counterfactual multiple objective optimization method; (iii) automatic skin cancer feature extraction utilizing feature squeezing, a deep learning-based feature selection technique inspired by the FS-SqueezeNet architecture, and (iv) classification using deep neural networks with K-nearest neighbors-based classification. Experimental evaluations utilizing the ISIC 2017 dataset demonstrated the proposed framework's superior performance, outperforming existing methods and achieving 96.88% accuracy, 96.94% sensitivity, 96.88% positive predictive value, 88.89% negative error rate, and 98.44% specificity in skin cancer classification tasks. The proposed framework shows great potential for integration into a mobile-based dermoscopic diagnosis system to detect abnormal samples and optimize computational resources for maximum efficiency.

We carried out a comprehensive study on the electronic properties of sodium using advanced computational methods. Our analysis focused on the single-particle density matrix and the Lefebvre-Brueckner-Wigner self-energy. By applying these findings to sodium's Fermi surface, we were able to visualize and quantify the quasi-particle lifetimes. Our results demonstrated that the relativistic effects have a minimal impact on the electronic structure of sodium. However, the application of the Brueckner-Gorkov Green's function Green's function significantly improves the description of the quasi-particle lifetimes over the standard Hartree-Fock approach, aligning with experimental data from angular-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Furthermore, the results are in line with the free-electron model predictions. Our evaluation of the density of states, Fermi velocity, and screening length also indicated that the relativistic corrections minimally affect these attributes in sodium.

In nonlinear physics, particularly in the study of free expansion expansion (FEE), a technique has been developed to analyze a six-dimensional phase envelope with six dimensions. This technique employs symplectic transformations based on units (STUs) to maintain phase integrity. By model the expansion process as a series of unit-free expansions and applying these transformations, we can calculate the evolution of correlations and entropies within the phase envelope. The effectiveness of STUs was verified through experiments and simulations to be a highly effective method for FEE and potentially other complex systems.

An interpretation of the weights of link graphs in terms of symplectic form measures is presented. This representation allows for the computation of Kontsevich weights of curvature graphs through integrated expressions that correspond to the weights. The results extend the existing calculations and build upon [KZ2]. The proofs rely on a fundamental transformation that expresses the product of two delta functions as an integral involving a derivative with respect to a graph-related function and a function of the symplectic form. This key identity combines a graph-related function with the inverse of the Laplacian matrix. The expressed integrals are the same as previously computed link graph integrals, enabling the conversion between symplectic and standard forms. The calculations were verified using numerical methods for specific examples.

We investigate whether high-amplitude, stable, and uniquely identifiable localized states can exist in woodpile and diatomic arrays, which have a disordered structure and reduced geometric frustration compared to the classic Frenkel-Kakadži (FK) arrangement. Our research involves numerical simulations of the Keller-Segel model, a sophisticated framework for analyzing array dynamics. These simulations have demonstrated that while isolated states can exist in certain variations of the FK model, their existence is generally precluded in the standard FK model. Our findings have however, identified specific circumstances in which isolated states can exist and persist in the FK model, particularly when there is minimal nonlinearity involved. These conditions have been confirmed to result in the emergence of stable localized states that can serve as precursors to patterns of standing waves observed in experimental settings.

Non-Gaussian patterns in cosmological fluctuations may serve as a signature from cosmological signals emitted during cosmological inflation. These patterns are often attributed to symmetries inherent to the de Sitter space, which is synonymous with the inflation period. This is achieved through the use of conformal features, a set of theoretical tools designed to generate and analyze the primordial fluctuations, often termed the "Cosmological Collider Physics." This paper aims to present a new set of techniques and perspectives in CCF, which not only provides a comprehensive framework for constructing feature-signals with distinct patterns, but also offers the possibility of deriving the conformal features, thereby facilitating a practical and PR-ready framework for the investigation of the primordials. Additionally, the new tools and patterns enable the design of the primordials signals, thereby facilitating a practical PR framework for the investigation of the primordials.

We've developed a criterion that determines whether the product of two graphs, specifically the lexicographic product, is Hamiltonian based on the existence of a perfect pairing in the base graph that results in a Hamiltonian accordeon within the fiber. Applying this rule to the product of $K_n$ and a quartic graph $G$, we found that it is Hamiltonian if and only if $G$ is also Hamiltonian. Furthermore, we established a condition based on the diameter and a perfect pairing that results in a Hamiltonian lexicographic product, even if the base graph isn't Hamiltonian itself. Testing this condition revealed that it's sufficient for a wide range of non-Hamiltonian graphs, but not all of them. Additionally, we examined the relationship between two specific types of graphs and found that an equivalence exists under certain conditions, while in other cases, the condition for equivalence appears more complex and dependent on perfect pairings.

We investigate the long-term dynamics and spectral properties of a non-symmetric quantum random walk on a three-state lattice, where the position operator exhibits discrete non-wandering behavior. This leads to a non-ergodic system with the absence of transport, where we examine how initial conditions affect wave packet evolution. Whereof, we demonstrate that certain wave packets follow a form of dynamical scaling over time. This is associated with the system's spectral characteristics, where we prove that the position expectation value's asymptotic behavior relates to the second moment of its absolutely continuous component of the spectral measure. Furthermore, under specific conditions, we establish that spectral types converge and type.

In recent years, self-attention mechanisms have been the primary focus in Vision Transformer (ViT) designs, but they lack the efficiency found in self-cueing mechanisms used in Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of self-cueing pools with CNNs, showing a 20% improvement in CNN performance. Although self-cueing pools have improved the performance of CNNs, they have yet to effectively boost the performance of ViTs. To address this, our study investigates the potential of employing self-cueing pools in ViTs to enhance the training process. We present a new variant of the self-cueing approach called Scan Attention (ScanAt), which uses self-attention-based features to improve the efficiency of ViTs. To effectively utilize its effectiveness, we developed a technique to generate self-cues directly from the image, rather than relying on handcrafted cues. When used in the ScanAt setup, our proposed technique significantly improved the efficiency of ViTs by approximately 2%, thus outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods.

A combination of dark energy and dark matter can be described by a single fluid model, which we examine in this work in the context of an expanding universe. We demonstrate that this description leads to a differential equation governing time-dependent velocity, that becomes simpler when combined with our proposed dissipative mechanism. This mechanism suggests that energy transfer occurs between the dark sector components. We analyze both the nature and rate of this transfer, showing that our model accommodates numerous previously established dark energy scenarios, including vacuum energy, quintessence, and quintessessence. We further establish that our model consistently results in a universe transitioning from accelerated expansion to decelerated expansion.

A simple direct proof of a theorem regarding incompressible Euler equations is provided, showing that a certain condition of convergence failure in Sobolev spaces holds for any degree above one. This proof is based on constructing a specific solution with vanishing angular momentum in a given geometric space configuration, leveraging the fact that such solutions diverge slowly over time according to a power law relationship. Furthermore, it is shown that although Sobolev norms of these solutions grow only at a rate of $T^{1/3}$, vorticity can exhibit significantly higher divergence while lower-order norms remain relatively stable. This fact invalidates the prerequisites of the main result of a study by al Mohyuddeen and Oh. A related discussion on the impact of VIGMAN's work on low-degree Sobolev convergence is also provided.

A significant number of text-to-image generation models utilize diffusion time-mapping to achieve desired results. However, this direct diffusion approach often leads to suboptimal image creation due to the persistent difficulty in optimizing diffusion processes. In an attempt to resolve these limitations, we introduce the Steady Creator (SC), a diffusion model framework based on the concept of generating images within a hidden realm. By establishing the SC's two fundamental principles, halting creation and guiding semantics, it outperforms prior methods while preserving semantic integrity. As the first generalizable framework for advanced diffusion models, the SC's performance is thoroughly validated through comprehensive evaluations and user studies across multiple tasks, showcasing its superior image quality and editability.

A new method for Bayesian Neural Networks, an innovative type of machine learning algorithm, is developed and applied to unrecoverable data modification. Unlike traditional concealment techniques that often result in lossy extraction, our approach utilizes a single-layer Bayesian model to achieve near-lossless reconstruction of original data. By training on various image types, the Bayesian model learns to identify and selectively alter specific bits, optimizing changes based on specific reconstruction goals. Compared to traditional methods, our approach offers improved accuracy and flexibility while allowing adaptability to different data formats without the need for format-specific parameters.

This study investigates the possibility that J/psi decays into invisible particles by analyzing neutral current effective field theories that incorporate light neutrinos and dark energy. To make the study feasible, we utilize data from the BaBar, Belle, BESIII, LHCb, ATLAS, CMS, and ALICE experiments. The analysis reveals that J/psi decays into invisible particles are possible within the framework of neutral current effective field theories with light neutrinos. Notably, the J/psi -> gamma + neutrinos channel appears particularly promising for future experiments. The study further finds that the neutrino coupling and lambda_1 effective parameters are linked and may reach values of O(10^-9) and O(10^-4), respectively. The data also implies that lambda_0 should meet a lower bound of O(10^-9) in models that include an unstable neutrino. The study in conjunction with future experiments could significantly advance our understanding of neutrino-based forces.

The presence of these features at the edge further implies that the magnetic structures are shielded from the corona, maintaining lower temperatures. In our investigation, we explore the significance of basic movements in identifying complex skills. Building on the work of Soltani and Golland's Dynamic Identification of Minimal Clips, we demonstrate that relying on specific key frames to pinpoint a target action is an unreliable method. Our study reveals that when using random selections of basic movements as input, the performance of the model remains consistent, indicating that the exact movement selection is unimportant. Furthermore, our research reveals two significant hurdles in using dynamic identification models for automated skill recognition. First, the reliance on pre-existing knowledge of skill execution is a limitation that hinders applicability in real-world scenarios. Second, the computational complexity and time-consuming nature of these models presents a major barrier to their practical use.

A new approach to shadow matter is proposed, which interacts through both gravitational forces and reversed electromagnetism with ordinary matter. Shadow matter's properties are explored under the assumption of stability due to conservation of charge in a two-component system, which would also indicate the absence of S-charge and make the force between it and ordinary matter repulsive. Shadow matter can condense into droplets due to its self-interacting force, resulting in a new interaction where it converts ordinary matter into electric current through a Lorentz force, enabling it to flow within the droplets and creating a net magnetic moment - effectively making it behave like a milli-magnetic monopole. This force between the monopole-like droplets can counteract its interaction with the galaxy's magnetic field, offering a solution to the problem of shadow matter accumulating at the galaxy's center instead of distributing throughout it, as well as potentially providing a source of the galaxy's magnetic field through the movement of the monopole-like droplets.

Extreme weather events pose significant threats to the environment and human safety, but the vast amount of historical data makes it challenging to analyze effectively. This research introduces SVP-Transformer, an innovative model that utilizes a Rich Model Memory and Rich Model Attention mechanism to effectively handle long temporal and spatial sequences in predicting severe weather patterns, thereby enhancing the model's capacity to capture essential climate patterns across various dimensions. Additionally, the concept of Dynamically Windowed Attention was developed to address computational constraints, demonstrating the model's remarkable ability to outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, the model was tested on two significant datasets: the open-access CERA-20T dataset and the stock market data, revealing its exceptional performance.

A model with three complex doublets and $S_3$ symmetry is proposed, offering multiple ways to achieve electroweak symmetry breaking. 
One method, 'dark matter option I', relies on an $S_3$-invariant potential, while 'dark matter option II', 'dark matter option III', and 'dark matter option IV', involve mixed $S_3$ and $Z_2$ symmetries acting on matter fields and scalar fields, respectively. 
In addition, we analyze the stability of these frameworks under small perturbations that break the $S_3$ symmetry. 
Furthermore, we explore the consequences of such perturbations on the neutral Higgs mass matrix.

A PPT quadrilateral hypothesis suggests that the set of PPT states forms a closed quadrilateral when combined with extreme BBMA states. We've found that, in contrast to its plausible counterpart, the PPT quadrilateral hypothesis does not hold as expected. We've demonstrated the existence of two BBMPA states whose combined effect contradicts the hypothesis, specifically showing they combine to form a PPT state outside the allowed set. Furthermore, we've discovered that BBMPA states can be combined in multiple ways to produce PPT states, essentially demonstrating that the set of PPT states lacks a convex-like structure according to the hypothesis.

Neural congestion is increasingly being seen as a key factor in neurodegenerative disorders. To better understand this issue, we aim to use controlled transportation methods in neurons to manage the accumulation of toxic substances within the cell. In our approach, the cell is modeled as a three-dimensional domain where various ions and molecules move through specific pathways in response to electrochemical forces. These movements are influenced by active and passive transport mechanisms as well as the chemical reactions taking place within the cell. From these dynamics, equations for substance concentrations are derived. These equations can be framed as optimal control problems, with the goal of minimizing a cost function that represents a balance between forced transportation and the damage caused by toxic substances. With the help of these cost functions, we can use the cell's electrochemical environment as a control variable to have a targeted effect on the movement of substances. This framework is further illustrated through simulations of specific ions in a typical cell shape and explores the potential benefits of utilizing endogenous transporters to manage transportation within the cell. Our results indicate that strategic manipulation of these converters can be used to prevent congestion in cells, a finding with potential applications in developing cell-targeted therapies for treating neurodegenerative disorders.

The analysis of large datasets has led to developing new data models that represent their structure. It's been discovered that certain characteristics from the original data significantly influence its behavior when it's processed. This realisation has sparked a significant shift from traditional data models to network analysis. As a result, researchers have developed new analytical tools and methods to study networks. Unfortunately, many of these tools and studies are confined to being published as research papers. This document aims to bridge this gap by presenting an extensive review of the most useful tools, their capabilities, and a comparison of the findings from contemporary research. Additionally, it suggests a potential area of application for one of the less explored network analysis methods, named Network Motifs. We outline a proposed approach to using Network Motifs to analyse the stock market as a network.

As a stellar object approaches a black hole's event horizon, time dilation will cause the accompanying emissions to be stretched out and shifted towards lower frequencies, a phenomenon that will cause the brightness of the accretion process to fade away.  It's anticipated that time dilation effects will dominate at frequencies above a certain point, called the turnover frequency, and this point will arrive earlier for black holes that form and a later stage for the black holes that don't form.  In cases where the black hole forms, the time when the accretion process starts to fade away due to time dilation will occur at a much closer distance, roughly a few thousand times the gravitational radius of the black hole, for black holes that form and occur at about a few million times the gravitational radius for black holes that don't form.  Any radiation emission coming from closer distances, a few times the gravitational radius, will occur when the white dwarf has a more intense interaction with the surrounding accretion disk and any radiation emission coming from further away will occur during the initial stages of the orbiting process and will occur at different times.  In any case, the final stages of the gravitational radiation emission from this process will take place at a different, faster rate and will occur many times more quickly than any accretion process.

We begin by establishing the theoretical framework to describe tau lepton decays involving three bodies, focusing on electromagnetic form factors within isospin channels. Our analysis involves a general step-by-step approach: initially, we identify all possible forms for the spectral function in isospin channels; next, we relate spectral function parameters to physical, measurable forms; finally, we connect spectral function constraints to relationships between physical forms. The derived relations serve as consistency checks and can also reveal connections between physical forms that experimental form factors may one day test. We highlight the significance of spectral function step $I^+_\mu J^-_
u$ in describing spectral neutron and proton form factors as well as the convolved two-body form factors of $\Delta G_{3/2}$ and $\Lambda G_{2,0}$. Our method also demonstrates that form factors associated with neutron and proton can be isolated by measuring tau decay modes $	au^- 	o n p  ar{
